profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:38:10.49+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
奉敕編集
後 學 天 台
按蕭子顯齊書崔祖思傳：宋朝初議封太祖為梁公，
祖思啟太祖曰：
「讖書云： 『金刀利刃齊刈之。 』
今宜稱齊，
實應天命。 」
太祖從之，
遂以齊建國。
太祖高皇帝
諱道成，
姓蕭氏，
字紹伯，
小字鬬將。
本居東海蘭陵縣中都鄉中都里，
晉惠帝分東海為蘭陵郡，
故為蘭陵郡人。
高祖整過江，
居晉陵武進縣之東城里。
時寓居江左者皆僑置本土，
加以南名，
更為南蘭陵人。
整生雋，
雋生樂子，
樂子生承之，
承之生帝。
建元元年(己未 、四七九)
是年四月受禪，
始改元建元。
正月，
甲辰 ，
以江州刺史蕭嶷為都督荊‧湘等八州諸軍事、荊州刺史，
尚書左僕射王延之為江州刺史，
安南長史蕭子良為督會稽等五郡諸軍事、會稽太守。
去年已命蕭映、蕭晃分鎮兗、豫矣。
嶷，
道成次子也；
子良，
道成之孫也。
江左之勢，
莫重於上流，
莫富於東土，
故又分布子孫以居之。
會，
工外翻。
守，
式又翻。
初，
沈攸之欲聚衆，
開民相告，
士民坐執役者甚衆；
嶷至鎮，
一日罷遣三千餘人。
府州儀物，
務存儉約，
輕刑薄斂，
所部大悅。
2 辛亥 ，
以竟陵世子賾為尚書僕射，
進號中軍大將軍、開府儀同三司。
道成進爵竟陵郡公，
故賾為竟陵世子。
賾，
七革翻。
3 太傅道成以謝朏有重名，
必欲引參佐命，
以為左長史。
嘗置酒與論魏、晉故事，
因曰：
「石苞不早勸晉文，
死方慟哭，
方之馮異，
非知機也。 」
晉文王薨，
石苞自揚州奔喪，
慟哭曰：
「基業如此，
而以人臣終乎！ 」
馮異勸漢光即尊位。
道成言石苞不能早勸晉文為禪代之事，
比之馮異勸漢光，
苞非知機者也；
欲以此言感動謝朏耳。
朏，
敷尾翻。
「晉文世事魏室，
必將身終北面；
借使魏依唐、虞故事，
亦當三讓彌高。 」
言三以天下讓，
則節行彌高也。
甲寅 ，
以朏為侍中，
更以王儉為左長史。
4 丙辰 ，
以給事黃門侍郎蕭長懋為雍州刺史。
長懋，
道成嫡長孫也。
5 二月，
丙子 ，
邵陵殤王友卒。
6 辛巳 ，
魏太皇太后及魏主如代郡溫泉。
7 甲午 ，
詔申前命，
命太傅贊拜不名。
前命，
見上卷上年。
8 己亥 ，
魏太皇太后及魏主如西宮。
西宮，
魏太祖天賜元年所築。
9 三月，
癸卯朔，
日有食之。
10甲辰 ，
以太傅為相國，
總百揆，
封十郡，
為齊公，
時以青州之齊郡、徐州之梁郡、南徐州之蘭陵、魯郡、琅邪、東海、晉陵、義興、揚州之吳郡、會稽十郡封。
其驃騎大將軍、揚州牧、南徐州刺史如故。
己
巳，
詔齊國官爵禮儀，
並倣天朝。
丙午 ，
以世子賾領南豫州刺史。
11楊運長去宣城郡還家，
齊公遣人殺之。
楊運長守宣城，
見上卷宋昇明元年。
蕭子顯齊志：臨淮郡有淩縣。
應劭曰：淩水出淩縣西南入淮。
酈道元曰：淩水出淩縣，
東流，
逕其縣故城東，
而東南流入淮。
義慶之孫也，
義慶，
長沙王第二子，
襲道規封。
「君先帝舊人，
身是宗室近屬，
如此形勢，
豈得久全！
若招合內外，
計多有從者。
臺城內人常有此心，
苦無人建意耳。 」
智即以告齊公。
庚戌 ，
誅綽兄弟及其黨與。
12甲寅 ，
齊公受策命，
赦其境內，
以石頭為世子宮，
一如東宮。
褚淵引何曾自魏司徒為晉承相故事，
求為齊官，
齊公不許。
以王儉為齊尚書右僕射，
領吏部；
儉時年二十八。
夏，
四月，
壬申朔，
進齊公爵為王，
增封十郡。
時又增徐州之南梁、陳、潁川、陳留、南兗州之盱眙、山陽、秦、廣陵、海陵、南沛等十郡。
甲戌 ，
武陵王贊卒，
非疾也。
史言齊殺之。
丙戌 ，
加齊王殊禮，
進世子為太子。
On the Xīnmǎo day, Emperor Shùn of Sòng issued an edict abdicating the throne in favor of Qí.
On the Rénchén day,
the Emperor was supposed to appear at the palace audience hall,
but he refused to come out,
fleeing instead beneath the Buddhist canopy.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
there had been a Buddhist chamber within the palace,
for the solemn veneration of Buddha statues,
with a precious canopy erected above to cover them,
and the Sòng Emperor fled beneath it.
They brought in a wooden carriage to welcome the Emperor.
The Empress Dowager, fearful,
personally led the eunuchs to search for and find him.
Jìngzé persuaded and urged him to come out,
leading him to ascend the carriage.
The Emperor, wiping his tears, said to Jìngzé:
"Are you going to kill me?"
Jìngzé replied:
"You will merely be moved to reside in a separate palace.
When your own family first took power from the Sīmǎ family, it was also like this."
The Emperor wept, snapping his fingers and saying:
"I pray that in future lives, for generation upon generation, I am never again born into an imperial family!"
Everyone in the palace wept.
The Emperor patted Jìngzé's hand and said:
"Do not worry excessively,
I shall reward you, the Fǔguó General, with a hundred thousand coins."
Jìngzé was then the Fǔguó General.
The historian states that the Emperor was mediocre and dim-witted.
All the officials attended in their positions.
The Palace Attendant Xiè Fěi was on duty,
and was supposed to hand over the imperial seal and ribbons,
but he pretended not to know,
saying:
"What official business is this?"
The messenger of the edict said:
"Hand over the imperial seal and ribbons to the Prince of Qí."
The messenger of the edict,
subordinate to the Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
entered and exited to proclaim imperial edicts and decrees.
Also, according to the *History of the Southern Dynasties*,
in commanderies and prefectures they were called "transmitters of instruction,"
while in the imperial court they were called "messengers of edicts."
Seal,
read as *sī shì fān*.
Ribbons,
pronounced *shòu*.
"Qí should naturally have its own Palace Attendant."
He then pulled a pillow over himself and lay down.
The messenger of the edict, alarmed,
wanted Xiè Fěi to claim illness,
intending to fetch a substitute,
intending to fetch someone to concurrently serve as Palace Attendant.
"I am not ill,
what is there to say!"
He then walked out in court robes through the Eastern Side Gate,
and still mounted his carriage to return home.
They then appointed Wáng Jiǎn as Palace Attendant,
to hand over the imperial seal and ribbons.
After the ceremony concluded,
the Emperor rode in a painted-wheel carriage.
A painted-wheel carriage is one
whose wheels are adorned with painted patterns.
The *Treatise on Carriages and Attire of Jìn* states: The painted-wheel carriage,
opens upward on four sides for viewing,
with green oiled curtains,
red silk netting,
the interior of the two compartments decorated with gold brocade,
coated with yellow gold,
in five colors.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: The lacquer-painted-wheel carriage,
with gold-coated crosspieces and ornaments,
is like a imperial carriage,
but slightly reduced in grandeur.
Dù Yòu said: According to Jìn regulations: For the imperial carriage, the wheel hubs are painted with colored lacquer,
with four upright posts rising above,
openings on the left and right for viewing on four sides,
green oiled crimson silk and blue interlaced netting above,
shaped like a imperial carriage,
its lower part still resembling an ox-cart.
The Emperor asked:
"Why are there no wind and percussion instruments playing today?"
None of those around him responded.
The Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Wáng Kūn,
was a younger cousin of Wáng Huá,
Wáng Huá had early on joined the establishment of the Duke of Sòng,
and assisted in governance at the beginning of the Yuánjiā era.
Blow/wind instruments,
read as *chǐ shuì fān*.
Cousin,
read as *cái yòng fān*;
the same below.
At this moment,
he clung to the carriage's otter-tail ornament, weeping bitterly.
Otter fur can repel dust,
hence it was hung on carriages.
"People consider longevity a joy,
but this old minister considers longevity a sorrow.
Since I could not lead the way for the ants,
meaning he could not die earlier.
He choked with sobs, unable to control himself,
and all the officials wept like rain.
Meaning their tears fell like rain.
In the first year of the Yǒngchū era of Sòng, they received the abdication from Jìn,
the year being Gēngshēn;
through eight rulers,
for sixty years, and then perished.
The Minister of Works concurrently Grand Guardian Chǔ Yuān and others presented the imperial seal and ribbons,
leading all officials to the Qí palace to urge the Prince to ascend the throne;
the Prince declined and had not yet accepted.
Chǔ Yuān's younger cousin, the former Administrator of Ānchéng, Chǔ Zhào, said to Chǔ Yuān's son Chǔ Bēn:
"Where is the Minister of Works today?"
Bēn replied:
"Presenting the imperial seal and ribbons at the Grand Marshal Gate of Qí."
Zhào said:
"I don't understand what your family's Minister of Works is doing, giving the possessions of one family to another family,
what is the point of that!"
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
the Prince assumed the position of Emperor at the southern suburban altar.
Returning to the palace,
he issued a general amnesty,
and changed the reign era.
He honored Emperor Shùn of Sòng as the Prince of Rǔyīn,
with preferential and lofty rituals,
all imitating the beginning of Sòng.
A palace was built in Dānyáng.
Dānyáng,
the *History of the Southern Dynasties* writes
"Dāndū".
Dānyáng is correct.
The *History of Qí* states: A palace was built in the old county of Dānyáng.
The spirit tablets of the Sòng emperors were moved to the Rǔyīn temple,
and all the princes were demoted to dukes;
except for those who had exerted effort for the Qí court,
all others had their fiefdoms abolished,
only establishing the three states of Nánkāng, Huáróng, and Píngxiāng,
to continue the lines of Liú Mùzhī, Wáng Hóng, and Hé Wújì.
The line of Wáng Hóng was not deprived of its state,
because Wáng Jiǎn had assisted the founding.
Píng,
is the same as "duckweed".
Píngxiāng County,
was established in the second year of the Bǎodǐng era of Wú.
Sòng Bái said:
When King Zhāo of Chǔ crossed the river,
he obtained a duckweed fruit here.
North of the present county are the Duckweed Fruit Lane and the King of Chǔ Terrace,
hence the county was named after it.
The officials of the two courts,
continued in their posts according to their appointments,
the two courts,
meaning the Sòng court and the Qí court.
Further detailed discussions would be held separately.
Chǔ Yuān was appointed as Minister over the Masses.
Guests filling the seats came to congratulate him.
Chǔ Zhào sighed and said:
"Yànhuí established a reputation for integrity in his youth,
who would have thought he would become so utterly unrestrained!
Unrestrained,
meaning defeated and running wild.
Defeated,
read as *pǔ pí fān*.
Youth,
read as *shī zhào fān*.
Integrity,
read as *xià mèng fān*.
And now he receives such an appointment.
If Yànhuí had died while serving as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
would he not have been considered a renowned scholar!
His virtue and reputation did not flourish,
yet he attained the longevity of a centenarian!"
The *Book of Rites* says: A hundred years of life is called the age of expectation and nurturing.
Zhèng's commentary states: Expectation,
means the essential;
nurturing,
means care;
not knowing about clothes and food flavors,
the filial son must merely exhaust the way of care.
The Court Attendant Péi Yǐ from Hédōng submitted a memorial,
enumerating the emperor’s faults and wrongdoings,
then hung up his official cap and left directly;
the emperor was enraged,
and had him executed.
A Court Attendant
merely attended court assemblies upon summons,
and held no substantive office.
Péi Yǐ, during the Sòng dynasty, held no office
nor possessed any outstanding or extraordinary integrity;
yet by refusing to eat the grain of Qí,
he thereby earned a lasting name in the annals of history.
A gentleman dislikes dying without his name being known,
precisely for this reason.
朝,
read as zhāo.
顗,
read as yǐ.
數,
read as shǔ.
The emperor said:
"Killing him would only complete his fame;
we should have simply disregarded him."
After some time,
he was dismissed from office and remained at home due to some incident.
The emperor inquired about governance from the former Acting Army Advisor Liú Huán of Pèiguó,
who replied:
"Governance lies in the Classic of Filial Piety.
All the reasons for the fall of the House of Sòng,
and for Your Majesty’s attainment of the throne,
are found therein.
If Your Majesty takes warning from the failures of the past,
and adds to it generosity and magnanimity,
then even in peril, stability can be achieved;
if you follow the same disastrous path,
then even in stability, peril is certain."
The emperor sighed and said:
"The words of a Confucian scholar
are a treasure for ten thousand generations!"
13 On Bǐngshēn,
the Wèi ruler went to Guōshān.
14 On Dīngyǒu,
he appointed the Crown Prince’s Household Manager Zhāng Xù as Central Drafting Official,
the Qí State General of the Left Guard Chén Xiǎndá as Central Protector of the Army,
and General of the Right Guard Lǐ Ānmín as Central Leader of the Army.
Xù
was the nephew of Zhāng Dài.
15 On Wùxū,

he appointed the Governor of Jīng Province Xiāo Yì as Director of the Imperial Secretariat, General of Agile Cavalry, Excellency with Equal Honors to the Three Ministers, and Governor of Yáng Province;
and the Governor of Southern Yǎn Province Xiāo Yìng as Governor of Jīng Province.
16 The emperor ordered his ministers to each speak on strengths and weaknesses.
The Grand Administrator of Huáinán and Xuānchéng Commanderies, Liú Shànmíng
(In Jiāngzuǒ, the Huáinán Commandery was established within the borders of Xuānchéng Commandery for émigrés,
hence Shànmíng governed both commanderies concurrently)
"requested the abolition of all harsh policies and minute regulations instituted since the Dàmíng and Tàishǐ eras of the Sòng,
to honor simplicity and ease."
He further believed:
"Jiāo Province is perilous and distant;
at the end of Sòng, governance was harsh,
leading to resentment and rebellion.
(In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng of Sòng,
Lǐ Chángrén occupied Jiāo Province and rebelled.)
It should be pacified with kindness and virtue.
Moreover, what that land produces
consists only of pearls and jewels,
which are hardly urgent necessities for our sagely court;
military campaigns against it
should, in my opinion, be halted for now."
The Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Cuī Zǔsī of Qīnghé, also submitted a memorial,
stating:
"If men do not study, they do not understand the Way."
(Words from the "Record of Learning" chapter of the Book of Rites.)
上,
read as shàng.
"Now, officials without established posts
receive salaries and labor service in vain,
depleting the people’s wealth.
(Officials without established posts are supernumerary officials,
what is referred to below as ‘persons beyond the limit’.)
(Lù refers to the salary they consume;
lì refers to the laborers they command.)
Have the supernumerary personnel in the central offices, commanderies, provinces, and princedoms each follow their inclinations
to study according to their chosen fields.
(In the Hànshū biography of Jiǎ Shān: ‘Make all devote themselves to their Way and elevate their integrity.’
The commentary states: Fāng
means the Way.)
樂,
read as lè.
Send them back to their native commanderies;
those exceptionally skilled in the classics and arts
should be treated without regard to regular promotion order.
Furthermore,
although Your Majesty personally practices frugality,
your subordinates still indulge in extravagance and luxury.
You should commend and promote court officials who are restrained, plain, pure, and cultivated,
and demote or dismiss those who are arrogant, extravagant, dissolute, and licentious;
then customs can be transformed."
During the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
all matters were entrusted to the commanderies and counties.
Emperor Shìzǔ, demanding swiftness,
found the commanderies and counties too slow,
and began dispatching imperial envoys to supervise them.
From then on, envoys were everywhere in great numbers,
vying to wield authority and power,
pursuing private gain and accepting bribes,
causing public and private labor and disturbance.
The Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, Prince Zǐliáng of Wénxǐ, submitted a memorial exhaustively detailing these abuses,
arguing:
"If the central offices have demands,
they should simply issue clear edicts and decrees,
setting deadlines,
and then people will think to exert themselves fully;
if there is delay,
they should be punished according to the statutes for investigation and accountability.
Now, although imperial envoys swarm in abundance,
they ultimately rely on the proper authorities to handle matters.
(Meaning that although the envoys are many,
they still must get things done through the responsible offices.)
Instead, they cause further obstruction and laxity.
All imperial envoys should be discontinued."
The Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Liú Sīxiào submitted a memorial stating:
"Since the Dàmíng era of Sòng,
gradual decline and exhaustion have been evident;
taxes and levies have increased while the imperial treasury has grown especially impoverished.
(Tiānfǔ refers to the emperor’s treasury.)
There is hardly any vitality left;
yet noble families and wealthy households
compete in extravagance and splendor,
to the extent that even the people of the mountains and marshes
dare not gather and eat the plants and drink the water.
Your Majesty should renew the royal regulations,
(Wáng dù means the royal laws.)
The emperor praised and rewarded them all,
sometimes forwarding their memorials to the outer court,
ordering the relevant officials to carefully select appropriate proposals
and submit them for implementation.
On Jǐhài,
an edict was issued:
"The various princes of the two palaces
are all forbidden to establish manors and estates
or enclose and seize mountains and lakes."
(The two palaces refer to the Upper Palace and the Eastern Palace.
The Upper Palace houses the imperial princes and sons;
the Eastern Palace houses the imperial grandsons.)
Dù Yù said: ‘Taking not by the Way is called lüè.’
He also said: ‘Lüè means enclosing boundaries.’)
17 The Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.

18 The Wèi Governor of Qín Province Wèi Luòhóu, Governor of Yōng Province Prince Mùchén of Yídū, and the Garrison Commander of Cháng’ān Chén Tí were all implicated for greed, cruelty, and lawlessness;
Luòhóu and Mùchén were executed,
and Tí was exiled to the frontier.
An edict was also issued stating:
"There are over a thousand surveillance officials.
(Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi established surveillance officials
to spy on matters inside and outside.)
For minor offenses, they nitpick and expose them,
(meaning they blow on hairs seeking flaws.)
We shall instead appoint several hundred careful and upright men,
to patrol the streets and roads,
apprehending only those causing disturbances and fights.
From then on, officials and people could finally pursue their occupations in peace."
19 Since the Tàishǐ era,
there have been many troubles both inside and outside,
and generals and commanders each recruited private troops,
stationing them in Jiànkāng.
Lǐ Ānmín submitted a memorial,
proposing
"that aside from the regular defenses north of the Huái,
all other troops should be disbanded and sent away;
(shū means to send.)
with limits set on their numbers."
The emperor followed this advice;
in the fifth month,
on Xīnhài,
an edict was issued to halt all private recruitment.
On the 20th day (Rénzǐ),
the Emperor rewarded the achievements of those who had assisted in establishing the dynasty.
Chǔ Yuān, Wáng Jiǎn, and others were promoted in rank and had their household registrations increased, each according to their merit.
A note of examination of discrepancies: The "History of the Southern Dynasties: Biography of Cuī Zǔsī" states:
"The Emperor intended to bestow the Nine Bestowals,
and both inside and outside the court, everyone supported it.
Only Zǔsī said: 'Your Excellency has upheld the state with benevolence and forgiveness,
adhering to the duty of a loyal minister.
A gentleman loves others with virtue;
it is not appropriate to act in this manner.'
The Emperor heard this and criticized him, saying:
'Zǔsī's words are far removed from what Xún Lìng would have said;
how could this be what I hoped for?'
From then on, he was no longer appointed to a substantive position,
but he was still treated with great respect.
Yuán Chóngzǔ received a secret decree
to consult with court officials.
The Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments, Yuán Hóng, said:
'I have received deep kindness from the Sòng house,
and I am also favored by Your Excellency's gracious treatment.
I dare not agree when advancing,
nor dare I differ when retreating.'
The General of the Champion Army, Cuī Wénzhòng, shared the same opinion as Chóngzǔ.
When the Emperor accepted the abdication,
Hóng retained his former rank,
while Wénzhòng and Chóngzǔ were both enfeoffed as marquises,
and Zǔsī was only given an additional official title."
According to this, when the Sòng dynasty first proposed enfeoffing the Emperor as the Duke of Liáng,
Zǔsī addressed Emperor Gāo, saying:
"A prophecy states:
'The sharp blade of the golden knife will cut down Qí.'
Now it is appropriate to adopt the name Qí,
as it truly responds to the Mandate of Heaven."
This was followed.
How then could Zǔsī have been completely loyal to Sòng?
This is now omitted.
"I have already completed writing the 'History of Qí,'
and the commentary states:
'Yuān was of a prominent family,
and Jiǎn was also a flower of the state;
they did not rely on their maternal uncles,
so how could they care for the state?'"
Diǎn
was the grandson of Hé Shàngzhī.
Hé Shàngzhī served under Sòng,
achieving high status during the reigns of Emperor Tàizǔ and Emperor Shìzǔ.
His stepmother was the Princess of Wújùn;
he also married the Princess of Bāxī.
Jiǎn's mother was the Princess of Wǔkāng;
he also married the Princess of Yángxiàn.
Therefore, Diǎn spoke in this manner.
On the 21st day (Jǐwèi),
someone rode a horse past the gate of the King of Rǔyīn,
and the guards were alarmed.
Someone pretending to be a rebel rushed in and killed the king,
then reported it as an illness.
The Emperor did not punish but rewarded them.
On the 23rd day (Xīnyǒu),
members of the Sòng imperial clan, such as the Duke of Yīn'ān, Xiè, were killed,
regardless of age, all were executed.
The former Governor of Yùzhōu, Liú Chéngzhī,
was the son of Zūnkǎo.
He was on good terms with Chǔ Yuān,
and Yuān firmly pleaded on his behalf,
saying:
"Chéngzhī and his brothers are not martial,
and they are also distantly related to the Liú clan."
Therefore, Zūnkǎo's clan alone was spared.
Zūnkǎo's younger brother, Sīkǎo,
had a son named Jìlián,
who later caused chaos in Shǔ.
On the 22nd day (Bǐngyín),
the Emperor's deceased father was posthumously honored as Emperor Xuān,
and his deceased mother, Lady Chén, was honored as Empress Xiào.
A note of examination of discrepancies: The "History of the Southern Dynasties" places this on the fourth month, Jiǎwǔ day.
Here, the "History of Qí" is followed.
On the 23rd day (Dīngmǎo),
the Emperor's son Jūn was enfeoffed as the Prince of Héngyáng.
The Emperor said to Yuán Chóngzǔ, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu:
"I have newly gained the realm,
and the Suǒ barbarians will surely use the pretext of sheltering Liú Chǎng
to invade our borders.
The southerners refer to the northerners as Suǒ barbarians
because the Wèi originally belonged to the Suǒtóu tribe.
Suǒ
is pronounced as xī gè fān.
Without you, there would be no one to control these barbarians."
Thus, Chóngzǔ was transferred to be the Governor of Yùzhōu.
In the sixth month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
the General of the Mobile Army, Yáo Dàohé, was executed
for his disloyalty to Shěn Yōuzhī.
This matter is recorded in the first year of Shēngmíng under Emperor Shùn of Sòng in the previous volume.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Crown Prince Zé was established as the Crown Prince;
the Emperor's sons: Yì was made the Prince of Yùzhāng,
Yìng the Prince of Línchuān,
Huǎng the Prince of Chángshā,
Yè the Prince of Wǔlíng,
Gǎo the Prince of Ānchéng,
Qiāng the Prince of Póyáng,
Shuò the Prince of Guìyáng,
Jiàn the Prince of Guǎnglíng;
and the Emperor's grandson, Chángmào, was made the Prince of Nánjùn.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Emperor Shùn of Sòng was buried at Suìnínglíng.
The Emperor, noting that the residents of Jiànkāng were mixed and disorderly,
with many villains and thieves,
intended to establish a household registration system to monitor and control them.
The Right Deputy Director, Wáng Jiǎn, advised:
"The capital is a place
where people from all directions converge.
If we must enforce household registration,
it will be troublesome in practice,
and in principle, it will not be comprehensive.
As Xiè Ān said,
'If not, how can it be called the capital?'"
The plan was then abandoned.
Earlier, when the Governor of Jiāozhōu, Lǐ Chángrén, died,
his cousin Shūxiàn took over the administration of the province.
As his orders were not being followed,
he sent an envoy to Sòng to request a governor.
Sòng appointed Shěn Huàn, the Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi, as the Governor of Jiāozhōu,
and made Shūxiàn Huàn's Níngyuān Military Advisor and the Grand Administrator of Wǔpíng and Xīnchāng commanderies.
In the third year of Jiànhéng under Sūn Hào of Wú,
the Fúyán barbarians were subjugated,
and their land was used to establish Wǔpíng commandery.
In that year,
Xīnxīng commandery was also carved out of Jiāozhǐ.
In the third year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Xīnchāng;
both belonged to Jiāozhōu.
Suí abolished Wǔpíng commandery and made it Lóngpíng county,
and abolished Xīnchāng commandery, making it Jiāníng county,
both under Jiāozhǐ commandery.
Táng changed Lóngpíng to Tàipíng,
still under Jiāozhǐ,
and made Jiāníng county the seat of Fēngzhōu.
As the people were obedient to Shūxiàn,
he mobilized troops to guard strategic points
and did not admit Huàn.
Huàn halted at Yùlín
and died of illness.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
an edict was issued:
"Jiāozhǐ and Bǐjǐng alone are cut off from the calendar,
meaning they reject orders and do not accept the orthodox calendar.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven would issue the calendar for the twelve months of the coming year to the feudal lords in late winter.
The feudal lords would receive it and store it in the ancestral temple.
At the beginning of each month, they would offer a special sheep in the temple,
request permission, and then implement it.
They have thus been led astray and have persisted in error.
A special pardon should be granted to Jiāozhōu,
and Shūxiàn should be appointed as its governor
to pacify the southern lands."
The Wèi commander of Jiālú garrison, Yáng Guǎngxiāng, requested to surrender.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Guǎngxiāng was appointed as the Governor of Shāzhōu.
Based on references from geographical records,
this Shāzhōu was likely established within the boundaries of Jǐnggǔ county in Lìzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
In the eighth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the Wèi Emperor went to Fāngshān.
Fāngshān is located north of Píngchéng on the Rúhún River.
The Wèi Emperor and Empress Dowager Féng intended to build their tombs there,
hence they visited the place frequently.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
The Emperor heard that Wèi was about to invade,
so in the ninth month,
on the Yǐsì day,
he appointed the Prince of Yùzhāng, Yì, as the Governor of Jīngzhōu and Xiāngzhōu,
with his military command remaining unchanged.
In the spring of this year, the first month,
Yì was appointed as the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
commanding eight provinces.
Now he was additionally appointed as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Minister of Works, Chǔ Yuān, was appointed as the Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Wèi appointed the Palace Attendant, Minister over the Masses, and Prince of Dōngyáng, Pī, as the Grand Commandant;
the Palace Attendant, Right Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Chén Jiàn, as the Minister over the Masses;
and the Palace Attendant, Imperial Secretariat, and the Dàirén, Xún Tuí, as the Minister of Works.
The "Treatise on Officials and Clans" in the "Book of Wèi" states: During the Shényuán period,
among the various surnames of tribes that entered from the remaining tribes, there was the Ruògān clan,
which was later changed to the Xún clan.
On the Jǐwèi day,
the Wèi Prince of Ānlè, Chánglè, plotted rebellion
and was ordered to commit suicide.
On the Gēngshēn day,
the Wèi Prince of Lǒngxī, Yuán Hè, died.
In winter,
On the Guǐwèi day (38th),
the Grand Consort of the Prince of Rǔyīn, née Wáng, passed away.
She was the Empress Wáng, consort of Emperor Míng of the Sòng.
After Emperor Shùn abdicated the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Rǔyīn,
and the Empress Dowager was demoted to Grand Consort.
39. Earlier,
a commoner from Jìnshòu, Lǐ Wūnú, along with Yáng Chéng of the Báishuǐ Dí tribe and others, raided Liángzhōu.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù notes: The Báishuǐ flows northwest from Líntáo County, originating from the Xīqīng Mountains to the southeast.
The water is white and turbid,
and flows southeast into the Yīnpíng region.
Dí people living along this river are called the Báishuǐ Dí.
(The authorities) attacked Chéng
and defeated him.
When the affair of Shěn Yōuzhī arose,
see the first year of the Shēngmíng era of Emperor Shùn of Sòng in the previous scroll.
(Lǐ Wūnú) claimed he was coming to assist,
but in reality, he was observing the situation.
After the affair was settled,
the court sent Wáng Xuánmiǎo to replace him.
An edict ordered Bǎinián and Wūnú to both come down (to the capital).
Wūnú urged Bǎinián not to accept the replacement;
Bǎinián had not yet decided on a plan,
when Xuánmiǎo had already arrived.
Bǎinián then left Wūnú in Hànzhōng,
and returned to Wèixīng,
lingering and not advancing.
The Left Guard Commander of Yùzhāng, Hú Xiézhī, once went to Bǎinián to request horses.
Bǎinián said:
"Horses are not dogs;
how can they meet endless demands!"
He treated the envoy very poorly.
When the envoy returned,
he told Xiézhī:
"Bǎinián said: 'What kind of dog is Hú Xiézhī!
His demands are insatiable!'"
Xiézhī resented him for this,
and slandered him to the Emperor, saying:
"Bǎinián relies on dangerous terrain and gathers crowds,
wanting to exclusively control a province."
The Emperor sent the Governor of Yōngzhōu, the Prince of Nánjùn, Chángmào, to lure Bǎinián,
proposing to appoint him as Prefectural Chief Clerk.
When Bǎinián reached Xiāngyáng,
the Emperor considered not questioning him,
but Xiézhī said:
"Having captured a tiger,
would you then release it back to the mountain?"
"Gé" means
to capture,
to fight.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Bǎinián was ordered to commit suicide.
Lǐ Wūnú rebelled and fled into Dí territory,
relying on Yáng Wénhóng.
He led over a thousand Dí soldiers to raid Liángzhōu,
capturing the Báimǎ garrison.
The Báimǎ garrison is north of the Miǎn River,
which is Yángpíng Pass.
Wūnú led light troops to attack the provincial capital city.
Xuánmiǎo set an ambush and intercepted them,
inflicting a major defeat.
Wūnú escaped with his life and fled back into Dí territory.
Earlier,
when Xuánmiǎo was Governor of Qīngzhōu,
in the early Tàishǐ era of the Sòng,
Xuánmiǎo held Pányáng to resist the Wèi,
and was therefore appointed as Governor of Qīngzhōu.
He was suspected by Emperor Tàizōng of Sòng.
See the events in the sixth year of the Tàishǐ era, scroll 132.
(Emperor Tàizōng) sent a letter to win over Xuánmiǎo.
Xuánmiǎo's Chief Clerk, Fáng Shū'ān of Qīnghé, said:
"General, you hold the heavy responsibility of a regional governor.
To abandon loyalty and filial piety without cause—
the gentlemen of Sān Qí
would rather tread into the Eastern Sea and die.
Since Xiàng Yǔ divided the land and established various kings,
dividing the Qí territory among three kings,
the Qí region was later called Sān Qí,
just as Guānzhōng is called Sān Qín."
Xuánmiǎo then did not reply to the letter.
Examination of discrepancies: The Nán Shǐ states:
"He then sent Shū'ān to present a memorial to the court to report this.
The Emperor (the future Emperor of Qí) arrested him on the road,
and also demanded Xuánmiǎo's memorial.
Shū'ān said: 'General Wáng's memorial is for the Son of Heaven,
not for the General (the future Emperor).
Moreover, what I have said
benefits the state, not the General.
There is nothing to ask me.'
Xún Bóyù urged the Emperor to kill him.
The Emperor said: 'Everyone serves their own master;
there is nothing to blame.'"
According to this, when Tàizǔ (the future Emperor of Qí) was a border general,
if he arrested Shū'ān
and did not kill him,
he should then have ceased to be a subject of Sòng.
The Qí Shū does not record this event,
so it is not adopted here.
(Xuánmiǎo) reached Huáiyīn,
marched his army straight through with strict discipline;
arrived at Jiànkāng,
reported to Emperor Tàizōng,
stating that (the future Emperor) had rebellious intentions.
When (the future Emperor) became Marshal of the Cavalry,
after Cāngwú was assassinated,
(the future Emperor) was promoted to Grand Marshal of the Cavalry.
Xuánmiǎo was very afraid,
but (the future Emperor) treated him as before.
After defeating Wūnú,
the Emperor said:
"Xuánmiǎo indeed did not betray my favorable treatment."
Shū'ān was appointed as Administrator of Níngshǔ.
In the early Yǒngchū era of Sòng,
Guànghàn was divided to create Níngshǔ Commandery.
(The Emperor) intended to appoint him as Governor of Liángzhōu,
but he fell ill and died.
40. In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnhài day,
the Crown Prince's consort, née Péi, was established.
41. On the Guǐchǒu day,
Wèi sent the Acting Prince of Liáng Commandery, Jiā, to supervise two generals advancing from Huáiyīn;
the Duke of Lǒngxī, Chēn, to supervise three generals advancing from Guǎnglíng;
and the Duke of Hédōng, Xuē Hǔzǐ, to supervise three generals advancing from Shòuyáng,
escorting the Prince of Dānyáng, Liú Chǎng, on an invasion.
In the early Jǐnghé era,
Chǎng fled to Wèi.
"Jiàng"
is pronounced "liàng";
the same below.
(Chǎng) inherited the fiefdom south of the Yangtze,
and became a vassal of Wèi.
"Zuò" means to establish an altar to the soil and grain;
also,
to guard the altar to the soil and grain is called "zuò".
In the first year of the Tàiyù era of Emperor Míng of Sòng,
(Chǎng) surrendered to Wèi.
"Qiú"
is pronounced "cíyóu".
A commoner from Yìyáng, Xiè Tiāngài, declared himself Governor of Sīzhōu,
intending to attach the province to Wèi.
The Wèi garrison commander of Lèlíng, Wéi Zhēn, led troops across the Huái River to respond.
Wèi established the Lèlíng garrison at Bǐyáng,
within the boundaries of present-day Tángzhōu.
Wéi Zhēn captured over seven thousand households and left.
Examination of discrepancies: The biography of Xiāo Jǐngxiān in Qí Shū states:
"Tiāngài colluded with and incited the barbarians.
Jǐngxiān reported this to the supervisory headquarters.
The Prince of Yùzhāng sent Huìlǎng to assist Jǐngxiān in attacking Tiāngài's partisans.
The barbarians soon sent their pseudo-Southern Department Minister, Lèi Bá, to station at Rǔnán,
and the Governor of Luòzhōu, the Prince of Chānglí, Féng Shā, to station at Qīngqiū.
Jǐngxiān made strict preparations to await the enemy.
The barbarians withdrew."
The biography of Wéi Zhēn in Wèi Shū states:
"Tiāngài appointed himself Governor of Sīzhōu,
planning to submit internally.
The affair was leaked,
and he was attacked and besieged by Dào Chéng's general Cuī Huìjǐng.
An edict ordered Zhēn to lead the garrison troops and horses across the Huái River to provide support.
At that time, Dào Chéng heard that Zhēn was coming,
and sent the general Xún Yuánbīn to occupy the Huái River and block Zhēn.
Zhēn fought fiercely from both front and rear,
and defeated him.
Tiāngài was soon killed by his subordinates,
who surrendered to Huìjǐng.
Zhēn advanced swiftly, taking advantage of the victory,
and again defeated Huìjǐng,
gathering over seven thousand surrendered households and moving them inward,
petitioning to establish Chéngyáng, Gānglíng, and Yìyáng commanderies to settle them."
According to this, the Wèi generals had no Lèi Bá or Féng Shā,
and Huìjǐng was also not the general sent to attack Tiāngài.
Probably the histories of the two states
each came from hearsay,
and mutually contained errors.
Now, the general outlines of the two histories are roughly combined and used.
(Jǐngxiān) was the Emperor's nephew.
The Governor of Nányǎnzhōu, Wáng Jìngzé, heard that Wèi generals were about to cross the Huái,
abandoned his garrison, and returned to Jiànkāng.
The soldiers and people were alarmed and scattered.
Afterwards, the Wèi army ultimately did not arrive.
The Emperor, because he was a meritorious official,
did not question him.
When the Emperor was assisting Sòng,
he sent the Valiant Cavalry General Wáng Hóngfàn as an envoy to the Róurán,
to arrange a joint attack on Wèi.
Hóngfàn traveled from Shǔ through Tǔyùhún, traversed the Western Regions, and only then reached them.
At this time,
over a hundred thousand Róurán cavalry raided Wèi,
reaching the frontier and then returning.
42. This year,
Wèi issued an edict ordering the Palace Secretariat Director Gāo Yǔn to deliberate on establishing laws and ordinances.
Although Yǔn was very old,
his will and knowledge did not decline.
An edict, because Yǔn's family was poor and his support meager,
ordered ten musicians from the Music Bureau to visit Yǔn every five days to entertain him,
provided meals morning and evening,
presented ox meat and wine on the first and fifteenth days of the month,
and monthly provided clothing, silk, and cotton;
when he entered for an audience, a table and staff were prepared for him,
and he was consulted on governance.
43 The Qìdān tribe's Mòhèfú Wùgān led over ten thousand households of his tribe to submit to the Wèi,
settling east of the Báiláng River.
The Qìdān chieftain is called Mòhèfú.
The Suí Shū states: The Qìdān and the Kùmò Xī are both of Dōnghú stock,
were defeated by the Mùróng clan,
and fled into the region between the Sōng and Mò deserts.
At this time, they were being invaded by Gāolì,
and sought to submit to the Wèi.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Báiláng River originates southeast of Báiláng County in Yòuběipíng,
flows northeast,
passes southwest of Lóngchéng,
then flows southeast,
and enters the Liáo River at Fáng County in Liáodōng.
The Chūxuéjì states: The Láng River flows down northeast of Huánglóngchéng,
which is the Báiláng River.
Qì,
pronounced qīqì fān,
also sounds like chī.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the first day of the month, wùxū,
a general amnesty was declared.
2 Appointed the Minister of Works Chǔ Yuān as Minister over the Masses,
and the Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Wáng Jiǎn as Left Vice Director;
Yuān declined the appointment.
An examination of discrepancies: The Qí Shū states,
"In the second year of the Jiànyuán era, first month,
appointed Yuān as Minister over the Masses.
Twelfth month, wùxū,
appointed Yuān as Minister over the Masses.
Fourth year, sixth month, guǐmǎo,
appointed Minister over the Masses Chǔ Yuān as Minister of Works.
Eighth month, guǐmǎo,
Minister over the Masses Chǔ Yuān passed away."
Yuān's biography states:
"In the third year, he was appointed Minister over the Masses,
but again firmly declined.
In the fourth year, due to illness, he resigned his position,
and was reassigned as Minister of Works.
Upon his death,
an edict stated: 'The Minister over the Masses has suddenly passed away.'"
It seems he declined in the second year, first month,
and accepted in the twelfth month.
The annals and biographies contradict each other.
3 On xīnchǒu,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice to the south.
4 The Wèi's Duke of Lǒngxī, Chēn, and others captured the Mǎtóu garrison,
killing the Grand Administrator Liú Cóng.
On yǐmǎo,
an edict was issued for strict military preparations throughout the empire,
mobilizing troops to resist the Wèi,
summoning the Prince of Nánjùn, Cháng Mào, to serve as General of the Central Army,
and stationing him at Shítóu.
5 The Wèi's Prince Zhuāng of Guǎngchuān, Lüè, passed away.
6 Wèi forces attacked Zhōnglí,
but the Governor of Xúzhōu, Cuī Wénzhòng, defeated them.
Wénzhòng dispatched his army commander Cuī Xiàobó to cross the Huái River,
attacking the Wèi garrison commander at Chíméi, Lóng Déhóu, and others,
killing them.
Wénzhòng
was a clansman of Zǔsī.
The Zhìmán barbarians relied on the mountain valleys for defense,
their territory spanning across the five provinces of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yǐng, and Sī.
Hearing that the Wèi army was invading,
they fully mobilized the able-bodied men.
The Nánxiāngchéng Mán barbarian Qín Yuǎn took advantage of the emptiness to raid Tóngyáng,
killing the county magistrate.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Zhì,
the Níngmán Prefecture administered commanderies including Nánxiāngchéng, Dōngxiāngchéng, Běixiāngchéng, and Zhōngxiāngchéng,
likely established based on the divisions of the Zhìmán tribes.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Cíqiū County in Huái'ān Commandery had the later Wèi's Xiāngchéng Commandery.
According to Shěn Yuē's Sòng Zhì,
Wènyáng Commandery administered the three counties of Tóngyáng, Jǔyáng, and Gāo'ān,

The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: In Jǔyáng County of Dōngwènyáng Commandery,
the Jǔ River originates from its northwest,
flows southeast past the north of Wènyáng Commandery,
which is within the boundaries of Gāo'ān County,

formerly a subordinate town of Xīnchéng Commandery.
In the early Yìxī era,
Xīnchéng was divided to establish this commandery,
its location should be west of Línjǔ County.

where waterways and land routes were winding and treacherous,
the routes passing through Mán and Dàn barbarian areas,

established Wènyáng Commandery to settle refugees.
The garrison commander of Píngchāng, Gǒu Yuánbīn, defeated them.

They reached Dāngyáng,

Jiàng,
pronounced jíliàng fān;
same below.
Qín Yuǎn fled far away.

the Emperor had the Grand Administrator of Qíjùn, Liú Huáiwèi, forge a letter from the Champion General Xuē Yuān to summon Dàobiāo;

All said:

his forces were several times larger than now,

Tàizǔ sent Prince Chángmào of Nánjùn and Prince Zǐliáng of Wénxǐ to convey an imperial reprimand,

ordering them to arrest Jǐngzhēn under the Crown Prince's command,
and execute him.
The Crown Prince, worried and fearful,
claimed illness.
After over a month,
Tàizǔ's anger had not subsided.
He lay resting in the Tàiyáng Hall during the day,
when Wáng Jìngzé entered directly,
kowtowed, and said to Tàizǔ:
"Your Majesty has ruled the empire for a short time,
and the Crown Prince has been reprimanded without cause.
People are fearful;
I hope Your Majesty will go to the Eastern Palace to resolve this."
Tàizǔ said nothing.
Jìngzé then loudly proclaimed the decree,
prepared to go to the Eastern Palace,
and ordered the imperial kitchen to prepare a feast.
He called for attendants to fetch the carriage,
but Tàizǔ showed no intention of moving.
Jìngzé fetched clothes and covered Tàizǔ,
then forcibly helped him onto the carriage.
Tàizǔ had no choice but to go to the Eastern Palace,
where he summoned the various princes to feast in the Xuánpǔ Garden.
Prince Huǎng of Chángshā held the huágài canopy,
(held also means to grasp),
and the pheasant-tail fan,
woven from pheasant tails,
used to shield the imperial carriage.
Prince Chángmào of Nánjùn served wine,
and the Crown Prince, along with Prince Yì of Yùzhāng and Wáng Jìngzé, personally presented wine and food.
By dusk,
all were drunk before returning.
Tàizǔ praised Bóyù for his loyalty,
and trusted him even more.
Secret military and state affairs
were often entrusted to him,
and his power shook the court.
When his mother passed away,
for about two lǐ from his residence,
officials and carriages already filled the road.
Left Guard Commander Xiāo Jǐngxiān and Palace Attendant Wáng Yàn went together to offer condolences.
From morning until evening,
they finally managed to approach.
By the time they left,
they were hungry and exhausted,
breathless and weary,
with frustration evident in their voices and expressions.
The next day,
they said to Tàizǔ:
"What we have seen at the gates of the two palaces
compared to Xún Bóyù's residence could have sparrow nets set up."
(Sparrow nets could be set outside the gate,
using the language of the Hànshū.
Yán Shìgǔ's annotation says:
"It means it is so quiet that no one passes by.")
(He was the nephew of Wáng Jìnghóng.
Wáng Jìnghóng was employed during the Yuánjiā era.
Cóng,
pronounced cái yòng fān.)
The Xiāoqí General Chén Yìnshū,
had previously also reported on Jǐngzhēn and the Crown Prince's faults,
but when speaking to the Crown Prince, he said
"Bóyù reported it."
The Crown Prince thus deeply resented Bóyù.
Tàizǔ secretly considered having Prince Yì of Yùzhāng replace the Crown Prince;
but Yì served the Crown Prince with increasing diligence,
so the Crown Prince's fraternal affection did not wane.
The Yùzhōu Governor Yuán Chóngzǔ did not closely align himself with the Crown Prince.
It happened that Chóngzǔ defeated Wei troops,
(see above, the third year of Tàizǔ's Jiànyuán era).
and Tàizǔ secretly plotted with him.
The Crown Prince grew suspicious of him,
and treated him with excessive courtesy,
saying:
"The rumors in the world,
I have already dismissed from my mind;
from now on, I will entrust you with wealth and honor."
Chóngzǔ bowed in gratitude.
It happened that Tàizǔ again sent Xún Bóyù,
instructing him on border affairs.
Bóyù received the order and set out at night,
unable to bid farewell to the Eastern Palace;
the Crown Prince believed he was not fully sincere,
and resented him even more.
On his deathbed,
Tàizǔ pointed to Bóyù, entrusting him to the Crown Prince.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Chóngzǔ was repeatedly promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
and Bóyù was repeatedly promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
Bóyù harbored inner worry and fear.
The Emperor, knowing Bóyù was on good terms with Chóngzǔ,
feared they might rebel,
and took special care to appease them.
On the Dīnghài day,
an edict was issued falsely accusing Chóngzǔ of recruiting unruly people north of the river,
intending to rebel with Bóyù.
Both were arrested and executed.

14. General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Jìng'ér was fond of believing in dreams.
When he first became the Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
his wife, Lady Shàng, dreamed that one of her hands was as hot as fire.
When he became Governor of Yōng Province,
she dreamed that one shoulder was hot.
When he was appointed to establish a headquarters,
she dreamed that half her body was hot.
Zhāng Jìng'ér's ambitions became boundless.
He often said to his close associates:
"My wife has now dreamed that her entire body is hot."
He also claimed that he dreamed the old village altar tree had grown high enough to reach the heavens.
The Emperor heard of this and was disgusted.
After Yuán Chóngzǔ's death,
Zhāng Jìng'ér became inwardly suspicious.
It happened that someone reported that Zhāng Jìng'ér had sent people to trade among the Mán tribes.
"Trade"
means commerce,
exchanging what one has
for what one lacks.
It happened that the Emperor was holding the Eight Abstentions Fast at the Huálín Garden.
These are Buddhist precepts: first,
do not kill living beings;
second,
do not steal;
third,
do not engage in sexual misconduct;
fourth,
do not speak falsely;
fifth,
do not consume alcohol or meat;
sixth,
do not wear garlands or jewelry,
anoint the body with perfumed oils, or intentionally go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or performances;
seventh,
do not sit on high or broad beds;
eighth,
do not eat after the noon meal.
The above are the eight precepts,
hence called the Eight Abstentions.
The Miscellaneous Records of Names and Meanings states: The Eight Precepts
are the one-day, one-night precepts observed by lay followers.
Called the Eight Precepts and One Fast,
collectively termed the Eight Abstentions Fast,
clearly meaning to prohibit and guard.
During the gathering, Zhāng Jìng'ér was arrested.
Zhāng Jìng'ér tore off his marten-fur hat and threw it to the ground, saying:
"This thing has ruined me!"
On Dīngyǒu day,
Zhāng Jìng'ér was executed,
along with his four sons.
Zhāng Jìng'ér's younger brother, Zhāng Gōng'ér,
constantly feared being implicated in his brother's disaster.
He resided in Guànjūn,
Guànjūn County,
which since the Hàn dynasty has belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
In the Táng, it became Líntuān County of Dèng Prefecture.
In our dynasty, in the early Jiànlóng era, Líntuān was abolished and merged into Rǎng County.
Guàn,
pronounced gùan.
His village was remote and secluded,
with layered walls and enclosures.
Whenever Zhāng Jìng'ér sent a messenger,
Zhāng Gōng'ér would mount his horse with bow and arrows ready,
and only then meet him.
When news of Zhāng Jìng'ér's defeat arrived,
he gathered his belongings and fled into Mán territory.
Later, he emerged on his own,
and the Emperor pardoned him.
Zhāng Jìng'ér's daughter was married to the son of Xiè Chāozōng, an Advisory Army Officer of the Northern Expedition.
Xiè Chāozōng said to Lǐ Ānmín, the Governor of Dānyáng:
"'Last year they killed Hán Xìn,
this year they killed Péng Yuè;'
Governor, what do you plan to do?"
Using the words of Xuē Gōng from the *Book of Hàn*,
he sought to incite Lǐ Ānmín
to start a rebellion.
The Emperor had long despised Xiè Chāozōng for his frivolity and disrespect.
He ordered Yuán Tuàn, who also served as Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, to submit a memorial impeaching Xiè Chāozōng.
On Dīngsì day,
Xiè Chāozōng was arrested and handed over to the Commandant of Justice.
He was exiled to Yuèxī,
and on the journey was ordered to commit suicide.
Because Yuán Tuàn's language was not severe enough,
the Emperor also ordered the Left Assistant Wáng Qūnzhī to submit a memorial impeaching Yuán Tuàn for drafting a frivolous and cursory memorial,
perverting the law and tolerating wrongdoing.
Yuán Tuàn was convicted and dismissed from office,
and barred from holding office for ten years.
Xiè Chāozōng
was the grandson of Xiè Língyùn;
Xiè Chāozōng
was the son of Xiè Língyùn's son, Xiè Fèng.
He was also the nephew of Yuán Yǐ.
Yuán Yǐ died during the Yìjiā rebellion.
Yǐ,

Earlier,

"Sēngqián will surely be a man of integrity,

24. Yú Luòhóu, the Governor of Qín Province in Wèi,
was by nature cruel and brutal.
When punishing people, he would invariably
cut off their wrists,
pull out their tongues,
and hang the severed parts on their four limbs.
The entire province was shocked and terrified.
The provincial populace, including Wáng Yuánshòu and others, rebelled simultaneously.
The responsible officials impeached him.
The Emperor of Wèi sent an envoy to the province,
who announced Yú Luòhóu's crimes to the officials and people at the usual place of his punishments,
and then beheaded him.
Qí Zhōu Regional Commander Hán Qílín,
prided himself on leniency in governance.
His aide Liú Pǔqìng advised Qílín, saying:
"You bear the official seals during the summer,
but have not enacted any executions.
How can you demonstrate your authority?"
Qílín replied:
"Punishments exist to stop wrongdoing;
humane officials use them only out of necessity.
Currently, the people are not breaking the law,
so what is there to execute them for?
If you believe that only through executions can authority be established,
then you, sir, should be the first to be executed!"
Pǔqìng stood up, ashamed and fearful.

Fàn Zhěn adamantly claimed there was no Buddha.
Zǐliáng said:
"You do not believe in cause and effect,
but the Buddhist teachings speak of cause and effect and retribution."
Zhěn replied:
"Human life is like tree blossoms opening together,
scattered by the wind: some fall upon curtains and cushions,
while others fall into dung heaps.
Those on the cushions,
that's you, Your Highness;
those in the dung,
that's I, the humble official.
Though the paths of the noble and the lowly differ greatly,
where then is the doctrine of cause and effect?"
Zǐliáng had no response.
Zhěn further composed the "On Spirit Extinction,"

"The form is the essence of the spirit,

The spirit to the body

This essay emerged,

6 The old system of Wèi: each household paid two bolts of silk,
two jin of cotton,
one jin of silk thread,
and twenty shí of grain;
also submitted an additional one bolt and two zhàng of silk,
stored in the provincial treasury,
to fund expenses beyond tributes;
the levies varied according to local produce.
On the day Dīng Mǎo,
an edict declared:
"The establishment of official ranks and salaries
has long been practiced;
since the chaos in the Central Plains,
this system was interrupted.
I, setting the pattern of ancient statutes,
have begun to disburse stipends.
The household levy increased by three bolts of silk,
and two shí and nine dǒu of grain,
for officials' salaries;
an additional levy of two bolts of silk externally.
After the salaries were disbursed,
those guilty of corruption with a full bolt will face death.
Change of law and adjustments,
worthy of a new beginning,
grant a great amnesty nationwide."

9 In September,

Three months make a season.
Violations worth ten bolts,
illicit earnings of twenty bolts,
were punished by death;
by this time,
illicit earnings of one bolt,
regardless of the scale of violations,
all faced death.
'Violations' referred to accepting bribes to alter judgments.
'Illicit earnings' described gifts exchanged privately for favors,
even without solicitation,
calculated and accounted for as corruption.
Officials and governors guilty of corruption were interrogated and dismissed.
Lǐ Hóngzhī, governor of Qín and Yì provinces, held eminence as an in-law,
as both Emperor Xiǎn and Gāo of Wèi originated from the Lǐ clan.
Wèi avoided using Emperor Xiǎn's personal name,
renaming Hóngnóng to Héngnóng.
After the distribution of salaries,
Hóngzhī was the first to fall because of corruption.
The Wèi emperor ordered him chained and brought to Píngchéng,
convened all officials to personally blame him;
yet, respecting his rank,
allowed him to resolve the matter at home.
Over forty local governors suffered death on charges of corruption.
None receiving salaries dare to move
without caution.
Bribes nearly ceased.
However, for officials and people guilty of other crimes,
the Wèi emperor generally showed leniency,
reducing many death penalties to exile to the border,
numbering in thousands annually.
In the capital, executions for major crimes,
were fewer than five or six per year;
provinces and towns were also rare.
After a long while,
Huáinán Wáng Tuó
petitioned to restore the former salary basis,
and Empress Dowager Wénmíng summoned ministers for discussion.
Zhōngshū Supervisor Gāo Lü believed:
"When hunger and cold are pressing,
even a loving mother cannot safeguard her son.
Now with salaries,
the honest have no excess,
while the corrupt are deterred;
without salaries, the corrupt can indulge in vice,
the honest cannot protect themselves.
Isn't Huáinán's proposal erroneous!"
The decree followed Lü's suggestion.
Lü further submitted,
asserting:
"The northern Dí are fierce and ignorant,
akin to beasts.
They excel in field battles,
but are weak in sieges.
The northern Dí,
referred to as the Ruǎnruǎn.
They cannot trouble us greatly,
nor can they penetrate deeply.
Moreover,
they wander and inhabit the wild lands,
following water and grass.
They arrive for battle with families and possessions,
flee with herds when they retreat,
needing no supplies as they are self-sufficient.
Thus, they have always been a border threat.
The six garrisons are divided,
doubling in force does not bring courage,
should the enemy double in strength,
garrison forces do not dare fight.
It is hard to control them.

many people concealed and falsely registered themselves,
with thirty to fifty families forming a single household.
The Palace Secretary Lǐ Chōng submitted a memorial:
The Secretariat was located within the palace,
hence it was called the Palace Secretariat,
also known as the Central Secretariat.
Shàng,
at that time, meant to submit.
"It is appropriate to follow the ancient system: establish a neighborhood head for every five families,
a village head for every five neighborhoods,
and a community head for every five villages,
selecting strong and prudent locals for these positions.
The neighborhood head is exempted from one man's corvée,
the village head from two men's,
and the community head from three men's.
If they serve without fault for three years,
they are promoted one rank.
As for the people's taxes,
for each husband and wife,
one bolt of silk,
and two dàn of grain.
Generally, ten bolts constitute the public tax,
two bolts for extra expenses,
and three bolts for officials' salaries.
Beyond this, there are also miscellaneous taxes.
For people aged eighty and above,
one son is allowed to be exempt from service.
For the orphaned, elderly, severely ill, and impoverished who cannot support themselves,
they are to be supported in rotation by the three heads within their jurisdiction."
The memorial was submitted,
and an edict ordered all officials to discuss it thoroughly.
The Secretariat Director Zhèng Xī and others all believed it was not feasible.
The Grand Commandant Pī said:
"I believe that if this law is implemented,
it will benefit both public and private interests.
However, this is a busy month,
and checking and comparing household registrations
will surely cause labor and resentment among the people.
I request that after this autumn,
in winter, envoys be dispatched,
which would be more appropriate for the matter."
Chōng said:
"'The people can be made to follow it,
but cannot be made to understand it.'
These are the words of Confucius from the Analects.
When levying taxes,
meaning the month of tax assessment,
if they do not see the benefits of equitable corvée and reduced taxes,
they will surely feel resentful.
It is better to implement it during the tax assessment month,
so they know the fairness of the tax system.
Once they understand the matter,
and also gain its benefits,
implementation will be easier."
Many ministers said:
"The nine-rank tax system,
has been in place for a long time.
The nine ranks,
are divided into three grades each for upper, middle, and lower,
as seen in the fifth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng of Sòng, in the 132nd scroll.
We fear it will cause disruption."
Empress Dowager Wénmíng said:
"Establishing the three heads will provide a constant standard for tax assessment,
concealed households can be brought out,
and opportunistic individuals can be stopped.
Why is it not feasible!"
On Jiǎxū,
the three heads of community, village, and neighborhood were first established,
and the people's household registrations were fixed.
Initially, the people were all distressed,
especially the powerful and wealthy who were unwilling.
Later, tax assessment and expenses were reduced by more than tenfold,
and both superiors and inferiors became content with it.
9 In the third month,
on Bǐngshēn,
Róurán sent an envoy Móutí to Wèi.
At that time, the Chìlè rebelled against Róurán,
and the Róurán Khagan Fúmíngdūn personally led a campaign against them,
pursuing them as far as the Western Desert.
The Western Desert
is the western part of the great desert.
Jiàng,
means to lead.
The Palace Secretariat Supervisor Gāo Lǘ said:
"In the Qin and Han eras,
the realm was unified,
so they could campaign far against the Xiōngnú.
Now, we have the Wú enemy to the south,
how can we abandon them to deeply enter the barbarian territory!"
The Wèi Emperor said:
"'Weapons are instruments of ill omen,
which the sage uses only when unavoidable.'
These are the words of Lǎozǐ.
It is because there are still unsubjugated barbarians.
Now that I inherit a peaceful reign,
how can I mobilize troops without reason!"
He treated the envoy with great courtesy and sent him back.
10 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Xīnyǒu, the first day,
Wèi first instituted the five grades of official robes;
on Jiǎzǐ,
for the first time, they used ceremonial robes and imperial carriages to sacrifice at the southern suburb.
Official robes,
are court attire;
the five grades,
are vermilion, purple, crimson, green, and blue.
Ceremonial robes,

11 On Guǐyǒu,
the Wèi Emperor went to Língquán Pond;
Wèi built Língquán Palace south of Fāng Mountain,
channeling the Rúhún River to form Língquán Pond,
one hundred paces east-west,
and two hundred paces north-south.
On Wùyín,
he returned to the palace.
12 The barbarians in Xiāngzhōu rebelled,

on Dīnghài,
Liǔ Shìlóng, the Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was appointed as Governor of Xiāngzhōu,

13 In the sixth month,
on Xīnyǒu,
the Wèi Emperor went to Fāng Mountain.

on this day, he visited Fāng Mountain.
On the seventh month, Wùxū, it also says he visited Fāng Mountain,

This is likely an omission in the text.
14 On Jǐmǎo,
Empress Dowager Wénmíng of Wèi bestowed a name on the imperial prince Xún,
and a great amnesty was declared.
15 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Wùxū,
the Wèi Emperor went to Fāng Mountain.

on Yǐhài,

jade pendants,
and large and small ribbon sashes to officials of the fifth rank and above in the Imperial Secretariat.
Ribbon sashes,

The Hàn system: For the seal sash, first twist single strands into one cord,
four cords make one fú,

five shǒu make one pattern,

means to organize.

is pronounced as shòu.
17 In the ninth month,
on Xīnmǎo,
Wèi constructed the Bright Hall and the Circular Moat.
18 In winter,
the eleventh month,
Wèi deliberated and decided that officials' salaries would be based on the number of households they governed.
The salary was determined by the number of households under their jurisdiction.
19 In the twelfth month,
Róurán invaded the Wèi border.
In this year,
Wèi changed the title of Zhōngshū Academy to Guózǐ Academy.
Wèi had initially established Zhōngshū Academicians and Zhōngshū Students,
now changed to Guózǐ Academy,
following the Jìn system.
There were thirty-eight provinces in total,
twenty-five in Hénán,
and thirteen in Héběi.
The twenty-five provinces in Hénán were
Qīng, Nánqīng, Yǎn, Qí, Jì, Guāng, Yù,
Luò, Xú, Dōngxú, Yōng, Qín, Nánqín, Liáng, Yì, Jīng, Liáng, Hé, Shā,
