Xiāo Zi Xiǎn said: "Yōng, Liáng, Qín, Shā, Jīng, Huá, Qí, Hé, Xīhuá, Níng, Shǎn, Luò, Jīng, Yǐng, Běiyù, Dōngjīng, Nányù, Xīyǎn, Dōngyǎn, Nánxú, Dōngxú, Qīng, Qí, Jì, Guāng are the twenty-five provinces in Hénán,
and Xiāng, Fén, Huái, Dōngyōng, Sì, Dìng, Yīng, Shuò, Bìng, Jì, Yōu, Píng, Sī are the thirteen provinces in Héběi."
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Dīnghài at the new moon,
the Wèi ruler decreed to set the music chapters,
and eliminate those not fitting the standard.
2 On Wǔzǐ,
Prince Yì of Yǔzhāng was appointed as Grand Marshal,
Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglíng was made Chancellor,
and Prince Yìng of Línchuān, General Wei Jiǎn, General King Jìngzé were granted the title of Kāifu Yitong Sansi.
Zǐliáng petitioned for Recorder Fàn Yún to be assigned a region,
to which the Emperor replied:
"I have heard he frequently shows off,
I will not pursue it further,
but should pardon and send him far away."
Zǐliáng replied:
"That is not so.
Yún frequently gives advice,
and the letters of remonstration are all kept."
He then presented over a hundred sheets,
with all straightforward and earnest words.
The Emperor sighed,
and said to Zǐliáng:
"I didn't expect Yún could be like this;
rather than sending him out,
he should assist you."
The Crown Prince Wénhuì once went to Dongtian fields to watch the harvest,
where at that time the Crown Prince worked on Dongtian, east of the Eastern Palace,
covering a vast area,
with magnificent views.
The Qi Annals recorded: The Crown Prince built tower halls at Mount Zhōng and called them Dongtian.
"This harvest is quite a sight."
The crowd all replied:
"Yes, yes."
Only Yún said:
"The work of the three seasons,
truly involves long toil.
The tasks of the three seasons,
being plowing in spring, weeding in summer, harvesting in fall.
Do not indulge in ease for a single morning’s pleasure!"
3 The wild man Huán Tiānshēng claimed to be from Huán Xuán's clan,
and stirred up the Yōng and Sī provinces' tribal people,
occupying the old city of Nányáng,
and requested troops from Wèi,
intending to invade.
On Dīngyǒu,
an edict was issued to grant Xiāo Jǐngxiān, prefect of Dānyáng, command,
leading both infantry and cavalry,
directly towards Yìyáng,
with the armies of Sī province all receiving his orders;
also granted General Chén Xiǎndá command,
leading General Dài Sēngjìng and others to move the navy towards Wǎn and Yè,
and all the armies of Yōng and Sī provinces received Xiǎndá's orders,
to suppress them.
4 Wèi's Nobleman of Xianyang, Gāo Yǔn, served five emperors,
namely Tàiwǔ, Jǐngmǔ, Wénchéng, Xiànwén and Gāozǔ.
In three departments,
the Department of State Affairs, the Department of the Imperial Secretariat, and the Department of the Imperial Library.
He was never once reprimanded;
Empress Dowager Féng and the Wèi ruler valued him highly,
often ordering Zhōnghuángmén Sū Xīngshòu to assist him.
Yǔn was benevolent and forgiving, simplistic and calm,
and though in a noble position,
he remained humble in conduct;
he held and read books continuously,
never letting them leave his hands day or night;
he taught others goodness,
with sincere and tireless dedication;
Yáng Zhōnglì said: Shunshun,
is entirely about sincerity.
Zhū Yuánhuì said: Shunshun,
is the appearance of truthfulness.
There was nothing he neglected.
Emperor Xiǎnzǔ conquered Qīng and Xú,
relocated the prominent families to Dài,
as recorded in Scroll 132 of the Song Dynasty, Míng Emperor's fifth year of Tàishǐ.
Displaced by hunger and cold;
Yǔn expended his wealth to relieve these needs,
allowing all to find their place,
and based on their talents and conduct,
recommended them to the court.
Many criticized them as recent followers,
but Yǔn said:
"Appoint the worthy and employ the able;
what does it matter if they are new or old!
If someone is useful,
how can they be suppressed for this reason!"
Yǔn was naturally free of illness,
but at this point he felt slightly unwell,
though he continued his daily activities as usual,
and after a few days passed away,
at the age of ninety-eight;
he was posthumously awarded as Palace Attendant, Sīkōng,
a generous funeral and mourning gifts bestowed.
Cloth is called Fù,
clothing is called Suì.
Fù,
pronounced as Fù.
Suì,
pronounced as Zuò Fān.
Those alive and those deceased all received gifts,
none unmatched.
5 Huán Tiānshēng led Wèi forces numbering over ten thousand to Bǐyáng,
Hàn's Bǐyáng County belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Yīng Shàu said: The source of Bǐ River.
During the Wèi Tàihé period, Dōngjīng Province was established at the old Bǐyáng city.
Sòng Bái said: Now Tángzhōu Bǐyáng county is the old provincial city.
The Nine Provinces Record: Bǐyáng County is seventy-five miles northeast of Tángzhōu.
Dài Sēngjìng Record,
Shēnjiǎo is forty miles from Bǐyáng.
Bǐ,
sounds like "bǐ".
Killing and capturing in the thousands.
Tiānshēng retreated to defend at Bǐyáng,
Sēngjìng besieged it,
but could not capture it and returned.
Wild man Hú Qiūshēng raised an army at Xuánhú to support Qí,
but the Wèi forces defeated him,
and Qiūshēng fled.
Tiānshēng again led Wèi troops to invade Wǔyīn,
where Wǔyīn garrison commander Yīn Gōngmǐn resisted and attacked,
defeating them,
killing their deputy Zhāng Qílín,
with Tiānshēng wounded and retreating.
In the third month,
on Dīngwèi,
Chén Xiǎndá was appointed governor of Yōng Province.
Xiǎndá advanced to garrison Wǔyáng City.
6 In summer,
in May,
on Rénchén,
the Wèi ruler went to Língquán Pool.
7 On Guǐsì,
Wèi Prince Nánpíng, Hún, passed away.
8 On Jiǎwǔ,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
An edict was issued to restore the five generations of ancestral temples
and those of the maternal kin;
they were exempted from taxes and labor.
9 Wèi's Official of the Ministry of the South, Gōngsūn Suì, and Duke of Shànggǔ Zhāng Shū led troops with Huán Tiānshēng to again raid Wǔyīn,
but Yīn Gōngmǐn broke their forces;
Tiānshēng fled back into the wilderness.
Suì,
was the grandson of Biǎo.
Gōngsūn Biǎo served Wèi under Emperor Míngyuán as a general.
In the state of Wei, there was a great drought in spring and summer,
with the Dai region being particularly severe;
additionally, an epidemic among cattle occurred,
and many people died of starvation.
In the sixth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
an edict was issued ordering officials both inside and outside the court to speak out frankly without concealment.
Hán Qílín, the Inspector of Qí Province, submitted a memorial stating:
"The wise kings of ancient times
stored grain for nine years;
in ancient times,
after three years of farming,
there would be a surplus of one year's food;
after nine years of farming,
there would be a surplus of three years' food.
Using the surplus of thirty years to regulate state expenditures,
there should then be a reserve of nine years.
If a state lacks a nine-year reserve, it is called insufficiency;
if it lacks a six-year reserve, it is called urgency;
if it lacks a three-year reserve, it is called a state that is no longer a state.
Rěn,
means a full year's harvest.
This practice was also esteemed,
with those who contributed grain being granted the same rank as those who beheaded enemies,
and those who diligently farmed receiving rewards equal to those for filial piety and fraternal duty.
The Hàn dynasty ordered the people to contribute grain in exchange for official rank.
There were also categories for filial piety, fraternal duty, and diligent farming.
Now, many do not farm,
and those who live off others without working
make up two-thirds of the population.
Since peace has lasted long,
and years of abundant harvests have accumulated,
people compete in showing off and boasting,
leading to extravagant customs.
Among wealthy and noble families,
even young maidservants wear fine clothing;
among merchant and artisan clans,
servants and slaves eat delicacies;
Zhāng Yàn said: 'Jade food'
refers to precious food.
Yet, silkworm-raising women lack coarse clothing.
Thus, the number of farmers decreases daily,
and fields lie fallow;
grain and silk are exhausted in the government storehouses,
while treasures and goods overflow in the markets and streets;
clothing and food are scarce in homes,
yet beautiful garments fill the roads.
The root cause of hunger and cold
truly lies herein.
I humbly suggest that all rare and exotic items
should be prohibited;
rituals for auspicious and inauspicious occasions
should be standardized with regulations;
farming and sericulture should be encouraged and supervised,
with strict rewards and punishments.
Within a few years,
there will surely be ample reserves.
In previous years, when households were registered and compared,
Máo Huǎng said: Guàn,
refers to village registers.
In Qí Province, which I govern,
the grain tax collected is barely enough to cover official salaries,
with almost none entering the granaries.
Although this benefits the people, it cannot last long.
If military campaigns arise,
or natural disasters occur,
I fear the means of supply
will have nowhere to turn.
We should reduce taxes on silk and cloth,
and increase the grain tax;
in years of abundance, store more,
and in lean years, distribute relief.
A year with reduced income is called a lean year.
Zhèn,
is pronounced as zhěn;
the same below.
Let reserves be stored by the government.
If the government has accumulated reserves,
then the people will have no years of famine."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
an edict was issued ordering the relevant officials to open granaries to provide relief loans,
and allowing the people to leave the passes to seek food.
The Wei capital was at Píngchéng,
and outside the suburbs and capital region,
checkpoints were established at key roads to inspect travelers.
The people were divided into those who left and those who stayed,
with provisions provided along the way,
and local officials caring for them at their destinations.
10 The Rúrú Khagan Fúmíngdūn was cruel and violent,
kě,
pronounced with a rising tone.
hán,
pronounced as hán.
and he was advised to make peace with Wei through marriage.
Fúmíngdūn became angry,
executed the advisor's entire clan,
causing his tribes to become disloyal.
In the eighth month,
the Rúrú invaded Wei's borders,
and Wei appointed the Minister Shàngshū Lù Ruì as Commander,
to attack the Rúrú,
defeating them decisively.
Ruì
was the son of Lì.
Lù Lì,
son of Lù Sì,
died during the troubles of Yǐ Hún.
Earlier,
the Gāochē leader Āfúzhìluó had over a hundred thousand tribesmen,
who were subjects of the Rúrú.
When Fúmíngdūn invaded Wei,
Āfúzhìluó advised against it,
but he was not heeded.
Āfúzhìluó became angry,
and together with his cousin Qióngqí, led their tribes westward,
reaching the northwest of the Qiánbù region,
where they declared themselves kings.
Examination of discrepancies: The Wèi Shū account of the Gāochē says this occurred in the eleventh year of Tàihé,
while the Rúrú account says the sixteenth year.
Here, the Gāochē account is followed.
Note: Under Rúrú, there should be
"account"
character.
"Hòulóufúlè,"
in the Xià language means Son of Heaven;
Qióngqí was titled
"Hòubèi,"
in the Xià language meaning Crown Prince.
Xià language,
refers to the language of China.
Xià,
pronounced as xià.
They divided their tribes and established themselves separately.
Āfúzhìluó resided in the north,
while Qióngqí resided in the south.
Fúmíngdūn pursued and attacked them,
but was repeatedly defeated by Āfúzhìluó,
and thus led his people eastward.
The historian notes that the Rúrú gradually declined.
Defeated,
pronounced as bài.
11 In the ninth month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
Wei issued an edict halting unbeneficial projects by the Ministry of Works,
which oversaw various artisans' affairs.
The Shū says: Let the hundred artisans arise.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
another edict was issued to stop the production of brocade, embroidery, damask, and gauze by the Imperial Workshop;
if the four classes of people wished to produce them,
they were allowed without prohibition.
The four classes,
are scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
Wei had been peaceful for a long time,
and government storehouses were full.

An edict ordered that eight-tenths of the clothing, treasures, miscellaneous utensils of the Imperial Household, carriages and equipment of the Imperial Stables, and bows, arrows, knives, and spears from the inner treasury
as well as clothing, silk fabrics, and silk wadding from the outer treasury
not needed for state use,
be distributed as rewards to all officials,
down to artisans, merchants, and lowly servants,
extending to the border garrisons of the six towns,
and within the capital region, widowers, widows, orphans, the childless, the poor, and the disabled,
each receiving according to rank.
Liú Xī's Shìmíng explains: A man without a wife is called a widower;
worried and unable to sleep,
his eyes often appear wide open.
The character is derived from fish,
as fish eyes never close.
A woman without a husband is called a widow;
widow,
means bare,
bare and alone.
One without a father is called an orphan;
orphan,
means to look around,
looking around with nothing to see.
One without children is called childless;
childless,
means like a deer,
a deer with nothing to rely on.
One without wealth is called poor.
Exhausted and ill is called disabled.
12 The Wei Secretary Gāo Yòu and Assistant Lǐ Biāo petitioned to change the state history from annalistic form to annals, biographies, tables, and treatises;
the Wei emperor agreed.
Yòu,
was the cousin of Yǔn.
In the twelfth month,
an edict ordered Biāo and the Editorial Director Cuī Guāng to revise the state history.
Guāng,
was the great-nephew of Dàogù.
The Emperor of Wei asked Gāo Yòu,
"How can we stop banditry?"
He replied,
"In the past, Sòng Jūn established virtue,
and fierce tigers crossed the river;
Zhuó Mào practiced transformation,
and locusts did not enter his territory.
(The affair of Sòng Jūn is seen in the 45th scroll, the seventh year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
Zhuó Mào was the magistrate of Mì County,
his teachings and transformation were greatly practiced.
During the time of Emperor Píng of Hàn,
there was a great locust plague across the land,
yet they alone did not enter the borders of Mì County.)
It is a matter of people.
If the local officials are the right men,
and governance and transformation are conducted properly,
stopping it is easy."
Yòu further submitted a memorial stating:
"In today's selection and appointment of officials,
we do not consider the excellence or inferiority of their understanding of governance,
but solely select based on the length of their seniority and service.
This cannot be called fully utilizing talent.
We should stop this superficial practice,
discard that outdated emphasis on seniority,
and promote officials based solely on talent.
Then the officialdom will become harmonious and upright.
(Fāng,
means the Way.
Mù,
means harmony,
and purity.)
Even if someone's years of diligent service are worthy of record, but their talent is not suited for pacifying the people,
they may be rewarded with noble rank and emoluments,
but should not be entrusted with regional responsibilities.
This is what is meant by the saying, 'A ruler may bestow wealth upon individuals as he pleases,
but he should not bestow official positions upon individuals as he pleases.'"

(That a ruler does not bestow official positions upon individuals as he pleases is a phrase from the concluding remarks of the Biographies of Flatterers and Favorites in the History of the Former Hàn Dynasty.)
Yòu was sent out to serve as the Inspector of Xīyǎnzhōu,
garrisoning Huátái.
Considering that while commanderies and kingdoms had schools,
counties and dǎng (local administrative units) should also have them,
he ordered counties to establish lecture halls,
and dǎng to establish elementary schools.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the yǐwèi day,
the Wei court issued an edict:
"For those who have committed capital crimes,
if their parents or grandparents are elderly,
and there are no other adult sons or grandsons,
nor any collateral relatives within the mourning period of one year,
a detailed report shall be submitted for consideration."
(Qīqīn refers to relatives for whom one observes the one-year mourning period.)
2. Previously,
the Imperial Prince, General of the Right Guard, Zǐxiǎng, had been adopted out to succeed Yùzhāng Prince Yí.
Later, Yí had a son of his own,
and submitted a request to keep him as his heir.
Whenever Zǐxiǎng entered court,
because his carriages and robes differed from those of the other princes,
he would often punch the walls of his carriage in frustration.
The Emperor heard of this,
and issued an edict that his carriages and robes should be the same as those of the imperial princes.
Subsequently, the relevant officials petitioned that Zǐxiǎng should be returned to his original lineage.
In the third month,
on the jǐhài day,
Zǐxiǎng was established as the Prince of Bādōng.
3. The garrison commander of Jiǎochéng, Zhāng Pú,
taking advantage of heavy fog, went by boat into the Qīng River area to gather firewood.
(Qīngzhōng refers to the area within the Qīng River.)
(Jiàng is pronounced jí liàng fān.)
The fort commander, Huángfǔ Zhòngxián, detected them,
led his troops to resist and fight them at the gate,
and barely managed to repel them.
More than 3,000 Wei infantry and cavalry had already arrived outside the moat.
The army commander of Huáiyīn, Wáng Sēngqìng, and others led troops to rescue them,
and the Wei forces then withdrew.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
Huán Tiānshēng again led Wei troops out and occupied Géchéng.
An edict ordered the Guerrilla General, Xiàpí's Cáo Hǔ, to supervise the various armies to attack him.
The Assistant General of the State, Zhū Gōng'ēn, led troops to reconnoiter and set an ambush,
encountered Tiānshēng's patrol troops,
engaged them in battle,
defeated them,
and then advanced to besiege Géchéng.
Tiānshēng led over ten thousand Wei infantry and cavalry to give battle.
Hǔ fought fiercely,
and inflicted a major defeat upon them,
capturing and beheading over two thousand men.
The next day,
they attacked and captured Géchéng,
beheading its Xiāngchéng Grand Administrator, Bó Wūzhù,
and again capturing and beheading over two thousand men.
Tiānshēng abandoned Píngshì City and fled.
(Píngshì was a Hàn dynasty county,
belonging to Nányáng Commandery.
During the Jìn and Sòng dynasties, it belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
Southwest of the county is Tóngbǎi Mountain,
the source of the Huái River.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Píngshì County of Huái'ān Commandery
was where Wei established Hànguǎng Commandery.
In the fifth year of the Kāibǎo era of our dynasty, Píngshì County was abolished and made a town,
incorporated into Bìyáng County of Tángzhōu.)
5. Chén Xiǎndá invaded Wei.
On the jiǎyín day,
Wei sent the Inspector of Yùzhōu, Tuòbá Jīn, to lead troops to resist him.
6. On the jiǎzǐ day,
Wei proclaimed a general amnesty.
7. On the yǐchǒu day,
the Wei Emperor went to Língquán Pond.
On the dīngmǎo day,
he went to Fāng Mountain.
On the jǐsì day,
he returned to the palace.
8. Wei built a city at Lǐyáng.
(Lǐyáng was probably north of the Lǐ River.)
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Lǐ River originates from Tóngbǎi Mountain,
sharing the same source as the Huái River but flowing separately.
It flows westward,
passes northeast of Píngshì County,
then flows west and empties into the Bǐ River.
They then attacked Bǐyáng.
The officers and soldiers within the city all wished to go out and fight.
The garrison commander Wéi Zhēn said:
(The Wei garrison commander of Lèlíng was garrisoning Bǐyáng.)
(Jiàng is pronounced jí liàng fān.)
"They have just arrived and their morale is keen;
we should not contend with them.
Let us instead firmly defend together,
wait until their strength is exhausted from attacking,
and then strike them."
They then relied on the city walls to resist and fight.
After twelve days,
Zhēn opened the gates at night and launched a surprise attack,
and Xiǎndá withdrew.
9. In the fifth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Liáng Míchéng, King of Dàngchāng, was appointed Inspector of Hézhōu and Liángzhōu.
10. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jǐchǒu day,
the Wei Emperor went to Língquán Pond,
and then proceeded to Fāng Mountain.
On the jǐhài day,
he returned to the palace.
11. In the ninth month,
on the rényín day,
the Emperor went to Lángyá City to review the troops.
(Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: The Southern Lángyá Commandery was originally administered from Jīnchéng.
During the Yǒngmíng era, its administration was moved to Báixià.
Shěn Yuē said: During the disorder at the end of Jìn,
over a thousand households of people from the Lángyá Principality followed Emperor Yuán across the Yangtze.
In the third year of the Tàixīng era,
Huáidé County was established.
Although Dānyáng had a Chancellor of Lángyá, it did not have the territory.
In the first year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng,
Huán Wēn held the commandery,
garrisoned at Jīnchéng on Púzhōu in Jiāngshèng,
and requested to carve out territory from Jiāngshèng County of Dānyáng to establish the commandery.)
12. On the guǐmǎo day,
the Wei Prince of Huáinán Jìng, Tuó, died.
The Wei Emperor was just then making offerings in the ancestral temple,
and had just begun the presentation,
when he heard the news.
He discontinued the sacrifice,
went to personally pay his respects, and was overcome with grief.
(Wèi is pronounced yú wèi fān.)
13. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the gēngshēn day,
it was the Beginning of Winter.
For the first time, he presided at the Tàijí Hall to read the seasonal ordinances.
14. In the intercalary month,
on the xīnyǒu day,
Wáng Huàn, the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was appointed General of the Central Army.
15. On the xīnwèi day,
the Wei Emperor went to Língquán Pond.
On the guǐyǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
16. In the twelfth month,
Gāo Gāozi, the Rouran garrison commander of Yīwú, led three thousand of his troops and surrendered the city to Wei.
17. The Emperor, because grain and cloth both within and outside the capital were extremely cheap,
adopted the suggestion of Lǐ Guīzhī, the Right Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat from Jiāngxià,
and disbursed fifty million coins from the upper treasury and also disbursed coins from the various provinces,
all to be used for purchasing grain.
18. The commander of Xīlíng garrison, Dù Yuányì, proposed:
"Wúxīng has had no autumn harvest,
while Kuàijī has had a bountiful harvest.
Merchants and travelers coming and going
are more than double the usual number.
The tax at the Xīlíng ox-dam,
according to official rates, is three thousand five hundred per day;
in my view,
it could be doubled daily.
Xīlíng is located at the present-day Xīxīng ferry, twelve li west of Xiāoshān County in Yuèzhōu.
King Qián Liú of Wúyuè considered 'Xīlíng' an inauspicious term,
so he changed it to Xīxīng.
The ox-dam is the present-day Xīxīng weir.
Oxen were used to pull boats,
hence it was called the ox-dam.
Dài (dam),
pronunciation: tú nài fān.
The southern ferry dam on the Pǔyáng River is the present-day Liánghú weir,
and the northern ferry dam is the present-day Cáo'é weir.
The Liǔpǔ dam is the present-day Kuàpǔ Bridge dam north of the Zhèjiāng Pavilion in Jiānggān, Hángzhōu.
Beyond the standard rates, an additional four million or so could be obtained.
If tax inspection at Xīlíng garrison is conducted beforehand,
it will not hinder garrison duties;
for the other three dams, I will personally appoint trusted men."
The Emperor referred the matter to Kuàijī,
where the administrator, Gù Xiànzhī of Wújùn, deliberated and believed:
"The original intention of establishing the ox-dam
was not to forcibly impose taxes;
rather, it was due to the swift and dangerous winds and waves,
to aid urgent needs and benefit the people.
Later supervisors failed to grasp its fundamental purpose,
each seeking their own merits,
either blocking other routes
or imposing empty taxes on river travel.
Considering that Wúxīng has suffered crop failures for years,
this year being especially severe,
the departure of people for more prosperous areas
is truly due to famine and urgency.
'Qù zhī'
should be
'qù fá'.
Jí,
means urgency.
According to the rates, reductions are not granted;
old rates have been newly reduced,
and no discussion has been held on increasing them,
yet now you propose to double beyond the rates—
by what means will this be achieved!
The Emperor's benevolent compassion for the suffering,
providing relief grain and exempting levies;
Zuǒzhuàn records: In Chǔ, during a great famine,
relief grain was distributed for shared consumption.
Dù Yù's commentary states: Zhèn,
means to distribute.
Lǐn,
means granary.
Diào,
pronunciation: tú diào fān.
To further increase hardship and distress,
is inhuman,
and has been condemned throughout history!
If actions do not match words,
fearing reprimand and interrogation,
they will inevitably resort to all manner of encroachments and hardships,
causing public resentment on behalf of the state.
Yuányì's nature is harsh and severe,
as demonstrated by past conduct;
to entrust him with such matters
is like setting a wolf to herd sheep.
As for those he wishes to appoint as trusted men,
they are likely tigers wearing official caps.
The Book of Documents states:
'Better to have ministers who steal than ministers who exploit and plunder,'
as recorded in the Dàxué, quoting Mèng Xiànzǐ's words.
Liǎn,
pronunciation: lì shàn fān.
The harm of exploiting the people is far greater.
I further believe that what is termed 'convenient and appropriate'
should mean convenient for the state
and appropriate for the people.
I have observed that recent proposals claiming convenience and appropriateness
do not utilize resources beyond the people's capacity
by harnessing heaven and dividing the earth;
harnessing the way of heaven,
dividing the benefits of the earth—
these are words from the sixth chapter of the Xiàojīng.
Instead, they bring inconvenience to the state.
Names contradict realities,
violating proper governance.
All such matters
truly warrant careful examination."
The Emperor accepted this and halted the proposal.
19. The Wèi sovereign consulted his ministers on methods to pacify the people.
The Secretariat Assistant, Lǐ Biāo, submitted a sealed memorial, believing:
"Among wealthy and noble families,
extravagance and presumption exceed proper limits.
Their residences, carriages, and attire
should be regulated according to rank.
Furthermore,
the rise and fall of a state
depends on the goodness or wickedness of the heir apparent;
the goodness or wickedness of the heir apparent
depends on the success or failure of instruction and guidance.
Zhǒng,
means great.
The Zhōulǐ commentary states: Zhǒng,
means the greatest among the great.
Zhǒng,
pronunciation: zhī lǒng fān.
When the heir is still young,
his disposition is not yet focused;
once he assumes myriad responsibilities,
he will have no leisure for review.
Reflecting on this today,
is it solely my fault,
or also the lack of diligence from the tutors?"
The Minister of Personnel, Lǐ Xīn, removed his cap to apologize.
This is a recent event that can serve as a warning.
I propose that we should follow ancient precedent by establishing official tutors
to instruct and guide the crown prince.
It was likely because Xún's lack of virtue had already become evident at this time
that Biāo made this statement.
Furthermore,
the Hàn established ever-normal granaries to relieve shortages.
See the twenty-seventh scroll, fifth year of the Hàn Emperor Xuāndì's Wǔfèng era.
Relocating people to prosperous areas
disrupts their livelihoods,
and only after hardship do they reach their destination,
which also results in actual losses
for the state's interests.
How much better it would be to store grain in granaries in advance
and distribute it peacefully—
is this not superior to driving and supervising the old and weak to seek sustenance a thousand li away!
We should allocate two-ninths of the regular levies from the provinces and commanderies,
along with surplus annual expenditures from the capital's revenue office,
to establish separate offices.
In years of abundance, purchase grain and store it in granaries;
in lean years, add a private markup of two and sell it to the people.
In this way,
the people will surely work hard in the fields to obtain official silk
and accumulate wealth to obtain official grain.
In harvest years, there will be constant accumulation;
in famine years, direct distribution will occur.
Within a few years,
grain will be stored and the people will have enough,
and even disasters will cause no harm.
Furthermore,
from among the people of the seven provinces beyond the river,
we should select those of distinguished family and talent,
summon them to the court,
and appoint them to official positions comparable to those in the central provinces,
according to their abilities.
The seven provinces beyond the river
are Qín, Yōng, Qí, Huà, Shǎn, Hé, and Liáng.
Based on the following text
'to win the hearts of those in Jiāng and Hàn to return to the way of righteousness,'
the seven provinces should refer to Jīng, Yǎn, Yù, Luò, Qīng, Xú, and Qí.
'Beyond the river'
simply means beyond the great river.
'Family talent' means
considering their hereditary status
and arranging them according to their talents and usefulness.
The central provinces refer to the capital region of Dàidū,
east to the sea,
south to the great river, and the various provinces.
Bǐ,
pronunciation: pí zhì fān,
means analogy or proportion.
This will also help win the hearts of those in Jiāng and Hàn to return to the way of righteousness.
Furthermore,
fathers and sons, brothers,
though distinct in body, share the same vital energy;
that punishment does not extend to one another
is the profound grace of the sovereign.
However, when it comes to sharing worry and fear,
this is indeed the constant principle of nature.
An unfeeling person,
whose father or elder brother is imprisoned,
shows no expression of grief or alarm;
whose son or younger brother evades punishment,
displays no look of shame or remorse;
who feasts peacefully in his honored position,
goes about his social engagements as usual,
with carriage, horse, clothing, and cap
unchanged in their splendid adornment—
is this what the affection between flesh and blood
ought to be!
In my humble opinion, when a father or elder brother commits a crime,
his sons or younger brothers should be made to wear plain garments and bare their shoulders,
and go to the palace gate to plead for punishment.
When a son or younger brother is implicated in a crime,
his father or elder brother should submit an open memorial accepting blame,
and beg to be relieved of his official duties.
If his position is essential
and such a request cannot be granted,
he should be comforted, encouraged, and retained.
In this way,
it would be sufficient to encourage and reform the shallow and indifferent,
making people understand what is shameful.
Furthermore,
when court officials suffer the loss of a parent,
upon the completion of their leave they return to their posts.
They wear brocade and ride in carriages,
participating in suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices;
with jade pendants tinkling and hat ribbons dangling,
they join in celebratory feasts and bestowals—
this injures the way of a filial child,
and damages the constant principles of Heaven and Earth.
I humbly propose that all who suffer the loss of a grandparent or parent
be allowed to complete the mourning period.
If there is no suitable person
and an official duty would be left vacant,
then a gracious decree should comfort and instruct them,
ordering them to resume handling affairs,
but only to oversee administration, disbursements, and submitting reports;
as for the state's auspicious celebrations,
they should have no part in them at all.
In cases of military alert,
they may serve in mourning garments of black hemp.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
Duke Xiāng of Jìn, while in mourning for Duke Wén,
wore black hemp mourning garments and cords and defeated the Qín army at Xiáo.
From that time onward,
serving in the military in black hemp mourning garments
(cuī,
pronounced cāng huí)
has been an appropriate practice."
The Wèi sovereign followed all of these proposals.
As a result, both the state and private households became well-supplied and prosperous.
Although there were occasional floods and droughts,
the people did not suffer hardship or poverty.
20. Wèi dispatched troops to attack Bǎijì,
but was defeated by Bǎijì.
Chén Shòu said: The Three Hán comprised a total of seventy-eight states,
and Bǎijì was one of them.
According to Lǐ Yánshòu's history,
its founders crossed the sea with a hundred families,
and later gradually grew powerful and established a state,
hence the name Bǎijì (Hundred Crossings).
During the Jìn period, Gāogōulì seized most of Liáodōng,
and Bǎijì also occupied the territories of the two commanderies, Liáoxī and Jìnpíng.

Cháng,

6 According to the old Wèi system,
the seasonal sacrifices at the ancestral temples were all held on the middle month of the season.
On Bǐngzǐ,
an edict was issued to begin using the first month of the season,

the ancestral temples had five annual sacrifices: the four first months and the winter sacrifice.
Wèi initially used the middle month,

7 Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng was appointed to oversee the Department of State Affairs.

On Wù
zǐ,

Chūxué Jì states: Zhōu Jǔ's letter, Cáo Cāo's Míng Fá Lìng, and Lù Huì's Yèzhōng Jì

and Qīngmíng is at the beginning of the third month;

Wèi previously used the Cold Food Festival to feast the ancestors,

Fù,

the fourth month,

This was because he wanted his sons not to bully each other based on rank or power.
(Obstructed)

In autumn,

Earlier,
Fúmíngdūn Kèhán of Róurán
(Kè)

(Peace.)
On the 18th day, the Wèi Minister over the Masses, Yù Yuán, and the Chief Minister of the Court for Dependencies, Yóu Mínggēn, repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement due to old age.

In winter,

The principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals

an event recorded in the previous year.

Passing through Jiǔjiāng.

"The fly-whisk and flyswatter

The Crown Prince was graceful and harmonious.

The Wei ruler ordered former general Yáng Bō to lead three thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry to serve as the rear guard.
At that time, the spring floods were just rising,

Bō formed a battle array on the southern bank to resist them,

The Qí troops converged from all sides and surrounded Bō.

They held out for two nights,

The Wei ruler, watching from the northern bank,

and the Emperor was pleased,
summoning the dukes and ministers,
showing them the memorial and saying:
"Rènchéng can truly be called a pillar of the state.
Looking at his legal arguments,
even Gāo Yáo could not surpass him!"
Turning to Xiányáng Prince Yuán Xǐ and others, he said:
"If you were in this situation,
you could not have handled it."
23 The Wèi Emperor planned to invade,
summoning the dukes and ministers to the Qīnghuī Hall,
saying:
"I have chosen the central region for our capital,
and the main framework is roughly established;
the Book of Documents says: Like a net attached to its main rope,
there is order without confusion.
见,
pronounced xiàn.
粗,
pronounced cū.
How can I imitate recent emperors who secluded themselves behind curtains in deep palaces!
I have decided to campaign south now,
but I am unsure of the exact timing.
Recently, all diviners have said
that if we go now, we will surely win.
This is a major affair of the state,
so ruler and ministers should each exhaust their views,
and not, because I spoke first, hesitate before me
and disagree afterward."
Lǐ Chōng replied:
"The method of employing troops
should first consider human affairs,
and then observe heavenly signs.
Now, although divination is auspicious, human preparations are not complete.
The capital move is still recent,
autumn harvests are not abundant,
and we cannot raise an army.
In my opinion,
we should wait until next autumn."
The Emperor said:
"Seventeen years ago,
I commanded two hundred thousand troops.
In the eleventh year of Qí Shìzǔ's Yǒngmíng era,
which was the seventeenth year of Wèi Gāozǔ's Tàihé era.
Wèi decided on moving the capital to Luòyáng and halted the southern campaign,
until last year when we invaded,
making it nineteen years.
'Two hundred thousand,'
should also be
'three hundred thousand,'
as seen in the events of the previous year.
去,
meaning past.
Also, according to the records, the claimed number was three hundred thousand,
but the actual was two hundred thousand.
And the heavenly timing was unfavorable.
Now that heavenly timing is favorable,
you again say human preparations are incomplete;
according to the Assistant Director's words,
there will never be a time for campaigns.
The enemy is at our doorstep,
and in the future, they will be a worry for the state.
How dare I rest easy!
If the autumn campaign is not victorious,
you all will be handed over to the Minister of Justice.
You must not hold back your thoughts."
Since Wèi established its capital at Luòyáng,
it was close to the Huái and Hàn Rivers,
hence the urgency to campaign south to expand the territory.
24 The Wèi Emperor, because many criminals exiled to the border had fled,
established a rule that if one person fled,
the entire household would be conscripted for labor.
The Governor of Guāngzhōu, Cuī Tǐng of Bólíng, submitted a memorial advising:
"In the world, good people are few,
and evil people are many.
If one person commits a crime,
and it extends to the entire household,
then Sīmǎ Niú would suffer the punishment for Huán Tuí,
and Liǔxià Huì would face execution for Dào Zhí.
Sīmǎ Niú was the brother of Huán Tuí,
and Liǔxià Huì was the brother of Dào Zhí.
They were all brothers.
The worthy and unworthy are far apart,
and brothers' crimes should not implicate each other;
this is ancient law.
魋,
pronounced tuí.
跖,
pronounced zhí.
The Emperor approved of this,
and abolished the rule.
Niè Chóngqí punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial order.
Later student from Tiāntái.
Gāozōng Míng Emperor, Part Two
Fourth year of Jiànwù (Dīngchǒu, 497)
1 Spring,
first month,
a general amnesty was declared.
Textual analysis note: The Qí Imperial Annals says:
"On Gēngwǔ,
a general amnesty was declared."
According to the perpetual calendar,
this month began on Jǐchǒu,
and there was no Gēngwǔ,
so no date is given.
2 On Bǐngshēn,
Wèi established the imperial son Yuán Kè as Crown Prince.
The Wèi Emperor held a banquet at the Qīnghuī Hall,
and when speaking of Crown Prince Yuán Xún,
Lǐ Chōng apologized:
"I am unworthy as a tutor,
unable to guide and instruct."
The Emperor said:
"Even I cannot reform his faults,
why should the tutor apologize!"
3 On Yǐsì,
the Wèi Emperor toured the north.
4. Earlier,
the Imperial Secretary Wang Yàn
had been favored and trusted by Emperor Shìzǔ.
(For details, see the seventh year of the Yǒngmíng era of Emperor Shìzǔ, scroll 136.)
Wang Yàn then gladly supported and served him.
(For details, see the first year, scroll 139.)
The Emperor once feasted with Wang Yàn at the Eastern Administrative Office,
and when the conversation turned to current affairs,
Wang Yàn clapped his hands and said:
"Your Highness often said that Yàn was timid;
what do you think now?"
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
Wang Yàn considered himself a meritorious official of the new dynasty,
and often criticized and belittled the old practices of Emperor Shìzǔ.
Once he held a leading position at court,
(the Imperial Secretary ranks above all other court officials.)
(Cháo,
read as zhāo.)
He placed his close associates in all important positions, both inside and outside the court,
and often argued with the Emperor over personnel appointments.
Although the Emperor needed Wang Yàn due to the circumstances,
(circumstances refer to the time when affairs were being carried out;
need means relying on him to be useful.)
he once sorted through Emperor Shìzǔ's imperial edicts
and found over three hundred handwritten notes to Wang Yàn,
all discussing state affairs.
He also found Wang Yàn's memorial advising Emperor Shìzǔ to have the Emperor take charge of official selection,
(see the eighth year of the Yǒngmíng era, scroll 137.)
(Xuǎn,
read as suàn.)
Shǐ'ān Wáng Xiāoguāng advised the Emperor to execute Wang Yàn,
but the Emperor said:
"Wang Yàn has rendered me service;
moreover, he has committed no crime."
Xiāoguāng said:
"Wang Yàn could not even remain loyal to Emperor Wǔ,
how could he be loyal to Your Majesty?"
The Emperor fell silent.
The Emperor sent his trusted confidant Chén
Shìfàn and others to patrol the streets and alleys,
gathering rumors.
Wang Yàn was frivolous and careless, lacking caution.
Hoping to be appointed to a high office,
he repeatedly summoned fortune-tellers to examine him,
saying he would achieve great nobility.
When speaking with guests,
he liked to dismiss others for private conversations.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he suspected Wang Yàn of planning rebellion,
and thus developed the intention to execute him.
The court attendant Xiānyú Wéncàn secretly discerned the Emperor's intent
and reported that Wang Yàn harbored treacherous ambitions.
Chén Shìfàn also informed the Emperor, saying:
"Wang Yàn plans to take advantage of the southern suburban sacrifice in the fourth year
to launch a surprise attack with the former commanders of Emperor Shìzǔ along the road."
At that time, a tiger trespassed on the suburban altar,
and the Emperor grew even more fearful.
One day before the sacrifice,
an edict was issued to halt the ceremony,
and Wang Yàn and Xú Xiàosì were informed first.
Xú Xiàosì obeyed the edict,
but Wang Yàn stated:
"The suburban sacrifice is a major event;
we must certainly exert ourselves."
The Emperor became even more convinced of Chén Shìfàn's words.
On the bǐngchén day,
Wang Yàn was summoned to the Huálín Bureau
and executed.
(The bureau was located in the Huálín Garden, hence the name.)
Commentary: Wang Yàn's biography states:
"After the New Year's court assembly, Wang Yàn was summoned and executed."
The Basic Annals state:
"On the bǐngchén day, Wang Yàn was executed."
The bǐngchén day was the 28th day of the first month.
Since the suburban sacrifice must take place in the first month,
and it is said that the ceremony was halted one day before the sacrifice,
then Wang Yàn's execution could not have been on the day of the New Year's court assembly.
His biography likely means after the New Year's court assembly ceremony.
Míngdá was likely a commander during Emperor Shìzǔ's time.
An edict was issued, stating:
"Wang Yàn, along with Yì and Míngdá, conspired to enthrall Hé dōng Wáng Xuàn, who is weak and incompetent,
making him a puppet ruler."
Wang Yàn's younger brother, Wáng Xǔ, was the Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
The Emperor sent the Central General's Adjutant Xiāo Jìchǎng to launch a surprise attack and kill him.
(Xiāo Jìchǎng was the Emperor's cousin.)
Xiāo Yì was extravagant and arrogant,
fond of archery and horsemanship,
which made the Emperor wary of him.
Thus, the Emperor used this incident to frame him.
(Xiāo Yì was a nephew of Emperor Gāo, the son of Xīnwú Hóu Jǐngxiān.)
(Hǎo,
read as hào.)
Therefore, he was not killed by the Emperor.
Hé dōng Wáng Xuàn, when attending court audiences,
often bowed deeply and hunched over,
not daring to walk upright or look directly ahead.
By this time,
as he grew slightly older,
he was implicated in Wang Yàn's case and dismissed from his post,
forbidden from communicating with outsiders.
Before Emperor Yùlín was deposed,
Wang Yàn's cousin, the Palace Censor Sīyuǎn, said to Wang Yàn:
"Elder brother, you received deep favor from Emperor Shìzǔ.
Now you suddenly assist others in such a matter.
They may use you for their schemes,
but I do not know how you will establish yourself in the future!
If you take your own life now,
you can still preserve your family's safety
and avoid a bad reputation later."
(He wanted him to die during Emperor Yùlín's crisis.)
Wang Yàn said:
"I am just eating porridge;
I have no time for this matter."
Later, when he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry,
(when the Emperor first ascended the throne, Wang Yàn was promoted to General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry.)
(Dàn,
read as tàn,
also read as tǎn.)
(Piào,
read as piào.)
(Qí,
read as jì.)
he said to Sīyuǎn's elder brother Sīzhēng:
"At the end of the Lóngchāng era,
Āróng advised me to commit suicide.
If I had followed his advice,
how could I be where I am today?"
Sīyuǎn immediately responded:
"As Āróng sees it,
it is still not too late now."
(During the Jin and Song dynasties, many people referred to their cousins as Āróng, a practice that continued until the Tang dynasty.
For example, Dù Fǔ's poem "Staying Up All Night at Cousin Dù Wèi's House"
says, "Staying up all night at Āróng's house.")
He took the opportunity to say to Wang Yàn:
"The times are somewhat different;
does elder brother realize it?
Most people are clumsy at planning for themselves but clever at planning for others."
Wang Yàn did not respond.
After Sīyuǎn left,
Wang Yàn sighed and said:
"There are actually people who advise others to die!"
Ten days later, Wang Yàn fell from power.
The Emperor, having heard Sīyuǎn's words,
did not punish him
and instead promoted him to Palace Attendant.
Wang Yàn's brother-in-law, Ruǎn Xiàoxù from Wèishì, also knew that Wang Yàn would surely fall.
(Wèishì County was under Chénliú during the Han dynasty.
During the Eastern Jin, it was established in exile in the area of present-day Liùhé County, under Qín Commandery.
The Ruǎn clan originally came from Wèishì, but they may not have lived in the Qín Commandery area at this time.
Wài dì means brother-in-law.)
He fled and hid, refusing to see Wang Yàn.
Once, he ate some delicious sauce
and, upon learning it came from Wang Yàn's household,
vomited it out and poured away the rest.
(He vomited what he had eaten
and poured away the remainder.)
Others feared for him,
but Ruǎn Xiàoxù said:
"We are relatives but not allies;
what is there to fear?"
In the end, he was not implicated in the crime.
5. In the second month,
on the rénxū day,
the Emperor of Wei arrived at Tàiyuán.
6. On the jiǎzǐ day,
the Left Executive of the Imperial Secretariat Xú Xiàosì was appointed Imperial Secretary,
replacing Wang Yàn.
(He replaced Wang Yàn's younger brother, Wáng Xǔ.)
On the 7th day, the Guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor of Wèi arrived at Píngchéng.
He summoned the faction of Mù Tài and Lù Ruì for an audience and questioned them.
Not a single person claimed to be wronged;
people of the time all admired the wisdom of Rénchéng Wáng Chéng.
Mù Tài and his close associates were all executed;
Lù Ruì was granted death in prison,
his wife and children were spared,
and they were exiled to Liáoxī to become commoners.
Textual analysis notes: The "Wèi Lǔ Zhuàn" in the Qí Shū states:
"The false General Who Conquers the North and Governor of Héngzhōu, Jùlùgū Hèlù Hún, defended Sānggān.
Hóng's paternal uncle, Píngyáng Wáng Ānshòu, garrisoned Huáizhà,
located northwest of Sānggān.
Hún, not being someone Hóng employed from the Central Plains,
conspired with the false Governor of Dìngzhōu, Féngyì Gōng Zìlín, and Ānlè Gōngzhǔ Tuòbá Āgān'ér to establish Ānshòu,
intending to divide and occupy Héběi.
The plan did not succeed for a long time,
and Ānshòu grew fearful,
so he reported to Hóng.
Hóng executed Hún and several hundred others,
and treated Ānshòu as before."
This account differs entirely from the Wèi Shū in terms of names and surnames.
We now follow the Wèi Shū.
Earlier,
when the Emperor of Wèi moved the capital,
changing old customs,
the Governor of Bìngzhōu, Xīnxīng Gōng Pī, was displeased with all of it.
The Emperor, considering him a senior member of the imperial clan and an elder,
did not force him either,
but merely guided him with the greater principles,
ensuring he did not create dissent.
He showed him the general direction of affairs and principles,
without repeatedly admonishing him.
Guide,
pronounced yǒu.
With officials in red robes filling the seats,
Pī alone wore Hú attire among them.
Only later did he gradually add a cap and belt,
but he could not properly adjust his appearance and demeanor.
The Emperor did not press him either.
When Crown Prince Xún was about to move from Píngchéng to Luòyáng,
Yuán Lóng and Mù Tài secretly plotted to keep Xún there,
intending to raise troops and cut off the passes,
planning to occupy the area north of Xíng.
North of Xíng,
refers to the lands of Héng and Shuò prefectures.
The passes,
refer to the Dōngxíng and Xīxíng passes of Yànmén.
Cut off,
pronounced dīng guǎn fān.
Xíng,
pronounced xíng.
Lóng and others informed Pī of their plot.
Pī outwardly worried about failure,
and though he verbally refuted and challenged them,
in his heart he rather agreed.
When the matter was discovered,
Pī accompanied the Emperor to Píngchéng.
Whenever the Emperor interrogated Tài and others,
he often had Pī sit and observe.
The relevant officials reported that Yuán Yè, Yuán Lóng, and Yuán Chāo deserved extermination of their clans for their crimes,
and Pī should be implicated.
The Emperor, because Pī had previously received an edict promising him exemption from death,
allowed him to be spared death and made a commoner.
He kept his later wife and two sons,
and they resided in Tàiyuán.
Lóng, Chāo, and their uterine brother Yǐshēng were executed.
Uterine brother,
means brothers from the same mother.
Earlier,
Pī, Ruì, along with the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Lǐ Chōng and the Commander of the Imperial Guard Yú Liè, had all received edicts promising exemption from death.
After Ruì was executed,
the Emperor bestowed an edict upon Chōng and Liè, stating:
"Ruì's rebellious intentions,
he brought upon himself from the netherworld;
the violation of the oath lies with him,
and is not related to Us.
Since rebellion is different,
even if We wished to show mercy for other offenses,
how could it be possible?
However, We still do not forget the previous words,
allowing him to die by his own hand in a separate residence.
He was not executed by being granted death at the office of the Governor of Héngzhōu but died in prison,
hence it is called a separate residence.
Execution.
The Shū·Gān Shì states: I will execute you and your sons.
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states: Nú,
means sons.
Sparing him from execution of his sons,
refers to Ruì's wife and children being spared death and exiled to Liáoxī.
Nú,
pronounced nú.
Being the chief instigator of the crime,
and implicated deserving death,
he was specially pardoned and made a commoner.
We originally hoped for constancy from beginning to end, but he himself abandoned and severed it.
Going against his heart and违背 his thoughts,
how lamentable indeed!
Therefore, We separately inform you of this,
hoping you do not find it strange.
Apart from the conspiracy to rebel,
everything is as clear as the bright sun."
Chōng and Liè both submitted memorials expressing gratitude.
Your servant Guāng remarks: Titles, emoluments, dismissals, and appointments,
life and death, granting and taking away,
these are the great instruments by which a ruler controls his ministers.
These are what the Zhōulǐ refers to as the eight instruments for controlling ministers.
Grant,
read as yǔ.
Even if they are relatives, old acquaintances, the worthy, the capable, the meritorious, the noble, the diligent, or guests,
if they have committed a crime,
they should not be pardoned outright;
they must be deliberated upon under the locust and thorn trees,
which is what the Zhōulǐ refers to as the eight considerations.
Locust and thorn trees,
symbolize the positions of the high ministers.
The Wángzhì states: When a case is concluded,
the Grand Minister of Justice hears it under the jujube tree.
If pardonable, then pardon;
if punishable, then punish;
if executable, then execute.
Severity should be weighed according to the circumstances,
leniency or strictness should adapt to the times.
Thus, the ruler can bestow grace without losing his authority,
and ministers can avoid punishment without daring to be presumptuous.
But in Wèi, it was not so.
Ministers of merit and nobility
were often预先 promised exemption from death.
When they became arrogant and committed crimes,
they were then executed.
This is using untrustworthy commands to lure them into a deadly trap.
Among the failures of penal administration,
none is greater than this!
8. At this time,
the old clans of the Dàixiāng region
were mostly involved in the conspiracy with Tài and others.
Only Yú Liè
was not implicated at all,
and the Emperor thus valued him even more.
The Emperor, considering that the northern tribal chiefs and their attendant sons feared the heat,
allowed them to come to Luòyáng in autumn for audience,
and return to their tribes in spring.
People of the time called them
"wild goose ministers."
This is because wild geese avoid the cold by flying south,
and when it warms up, they fly back north.
Audience,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
9. In the third month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
the Emperor of Wèi traveled south and reached Líshí.
Líshí,
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonged to the Xīhé commandery.
In Suí, it became Líshí commandery,
and in Táng, Shízhōu.
An edict was issued to pardon them.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
he reached Lóngmén,
and sent an envoy to offer sacrifices to Xià Yǔ.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The upper entrance of Lóngmén is west of Qū county in Hédōng commandery of Hàn,
which is the so-called Mèngmén.
The lower entrance of Lóngmén is northwest of Píshì county in Hédōng,
excavated by Great Yǔ,
hence sacrifices were offered here.
On the Guǐhài day,
he reached Púbǎn,
and offered sacrifices to Yú Shùn.
Huángfǔ Mì said: Shùn's capital was at Púbǎn,
hence sacrifices were also offered here.
Bǎn,
pronounced fǎn.
On the Xīnwèi day,
he reached Cháng'ān.
10. After Crown Prince Xún of Wèi was deposed,
he deeply regretted his actions.
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Biāo secretly memorialized that Xún was again conspiring with his attendants to rebel.
The Emperor of Wèi sent the Vice Director of the Central Secretariat Xíng Luán and Xiányáng Wáng Xí to carry an edict with pepper wine to Héyáng,
and bestowed death upon Xún.
Pepper is pungent in taste,
very heating,
and toxic,
especially the closed-mouth variety.
During the deliberation concerning Empress Huánsī of Hàn,
Lǐ Xián carried ground pepper with him;
the Emperor boiled two hú of pepper
to kill the descendants of Gāo and Wǔ;
it was the same substance.
He was buried at Héyáng.
11. On the Guǐwèi day,
the Grand General of Wèi, Sòngmíng Wáng Liú Chǎng, died at Péngchéng,
and was buried
with special honors.
The interpretation of the posthumous title "Míng": "Thoughtful and far-sighted is called Míng."
This means Chǎng had far-sighted plans,
and resolutely fled hardship to return to Wèi.
On the twelfth day of the fifth month,
the day Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor of Wèi returned eastward,
sailing along the Wèi River and entering the Huáng Hé.
On the day Rénchén,
he sent an envoy to offer sacrifices to King Wén of Zhōu at Fēng
and to King Wǔ at Hào.
This was also to perform sacrifices at the former capitals.
The Zhōu dynasty's Fēng and Hào
were entirely within the Shànglín Park during the Hàn period.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
On the day Gēngshēn,
he returned to Luòyáng.
On the thirteenth day, Rénxū,
Wèi mobilized two hundred thousand troops from the five provinces of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Xiàng, and Jǐ.
In the eighth year of the Tàicháng era of Emperor Tàizōng of Wèi,
Jǐ Province was established at the Qiáo'áo Fortress in Jǐběi,
governing the commanderies of Jǐběi, Píngyuán, Dōngpíng, and Nán Qīnghé.
Xiàng,
read as xī liàng fān.
Jǐ,
read as zǐ lǐ fān.
14. When Mù Tài of Wèi rebelled,
the Palace Secretariat Supervisor and Duke of Wèijùn, Mù Pí, conspired with him.
After the pardon, the matter was exposed,
and he was stripped of his official positions and noble rank, becoming a commoner.
Mù Pí's younger brother, the Minister of Works Mù Liàng, entrusted the affairs of his office to his Adjutant, Mùróng Qì,
and submitted a memorial impeaching himself.
The Emperor of Wèi issued a gracious edict not permitting it;
but Mù Liàng persistently requested without cease.
On the day Guǐhài,
the Emperor allowed Mù Liàng to retire from his position.
15. On the day Dīngmǎo,
Wèi divided its six armies to determine which would campaign and which would remain.
16. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wèi established the Lady Féng, a Zhaoyi (昭儀), as Empress.
The Empress wished to act as mother and raise the Crown Prince, Tuò.
Tuò's birth mother, Lady Gāo, traveled from Dài to Luòyáng,
but died suddenly in Gòng County.
The Zhaoyi Féng had already slandered and caused the deposition of her younger sister,
and now secretly killed the Crown Prince's mother.
Her heart was likely that of an owl or a jìng-beast.
With the Emperor of Wèi's intelligence,
to have her established in the position of Empress,
it would be fortunate if he did not one day die by her hand.
Gòng County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
During the Jìn and later Wèi dynasties, it belonged to Jí Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, it was part of Wèi Prefecture;
Gòngchéng County is its location.
Gòng,
pronounced gōng.
17. On the day Wùchén,
Wèi appointed Mù Liàng as Grand General Who Conquers the North, Holder of the Third Rank with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, and Governor of Jì Province.
18. In the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Wèi issued an edict for internal and external military preparedness.
This was in preparation for a southern campaign.
19. On the day Rénxū,
Wèi enfeoffed the imperial son Yú as Prince of Jīngzhào,
Yì as Prince of Qīnghé,
and Huái as Prince of Guǎngpíng.
20. He posthumously honored Wáng shì, the birth mother of the late Emperor Jǐng, as Empress Dowager Gōng.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he honored the late Prince of Shǐ'ān, Zhēn, as Emperor Jǐng.
Using "Emperor" (皇) and not "Sovereign" (帝)
follows the Hàn system.
21. On the day Jiǎxū,
Wèi conducted military exercises at the Huálín Garden;
on the day Gēngchén,
the army departed from Luòyáng.
He had the Minister of Personnel, the Prince of Rènchéng, Chéng, remain to guard the capital;
the Prince of Rènchéng, Chéng, only at this point became the substantive Minister of Personnel.
Shǒu,
read as shì yòu fān.
"Zhōngchéng"
should be
"Zhōngwèi".
【Chapter note: The twelve-line edition correctly has
"Zhōngwèi";
the Kǒng edition is the same;
the Zhāng collation is the same.
】 Dù,
read as tuó luò fān.
He provisionally appointed the Prince of Péngchéng, Xié, as Grand General of the Central Army.
Xié declined, saying:
"Employing both the close and the distant
is the way of antiquity.
What kind of person am I alone,
to receive such frequent and gracious appointments!
In the past, Chénsī sought but was not granted,
during the time of Emperor Wén of Cáo Wèi,
Chénsī Wáng Cáo Zhí submitted a memorial requesting to be tested in attacking Wú and Shǔ,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
How far apart are denial and favor!
When heaven and earth interact, it is called Tài (favor);
when heaven and earth do not interact, it is called Pǐ (denial).
Between Chénsī and Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the feelings of superior and subordinate did not communicate,
hence it was Pǐ.
For Xié, the feelings between ruler and minister, and between brothers, are without gap,
hence it is Tài.
Pǐ,
read as pí bǐ fān.
[The Emperor] took Xié's hand and said:
"The two Cáos harbored jealousy due to their talent and fame,
the two Cáos,

do not be deceived by petty men,
and become a laughingstock for posterity.
Yōngzhōu has already carefully considered this,
I hope you will make good plans!"
Yì did not agree.
Yǎn then welcomed his younger brothers, the Army Adjutant of the Cavalry General, Xiāo Wěi, and the Army Adjutant of the General of the Western Headquarters, Xiāo Dàn, to Xiāngyáng.
Initially,
although Emperor Gāozōng entrusted his final commands to the various lords,
he placed much trust in the brothers Jiāng Shí.
The final commands are recorded in the previous scroll, last year.
The brothers Jiāng Shí and Jiāng Sì
were nephews of Emperor Gāozōng's mother, Empress Jǐng,
hence he entrusted them with his confidence.
Every action and decision involved them.
The Emperor gradually wished to act according to his own will,
Xú Xiàosì could not oppose him,
Xiāo Tǎnzhī sometimes had differing opinions,
but Shí firmly held to the established regulations;
the Emperor deeply resented him.
The Emperor's attendants, such as Ruìjī's Rú Fǎzhēn and Wúxīng's Méi Chóng'ér,
were trusted and appointed by the Emperor,
but Shí often restrained and opposed them;
Fǎzhēn and the others gnashed their teeth in hatred.
Xú Xiàosì said to Shí:
"The ruler has slightly different views,
how can we completely oppose and contradict him!"
To establish a different view is to be "guāi,"
not to follow his will is to be "fǎn."
"Just leave it to me,
and you will have nothing to worry about."
The emperor’s lack of virtue became increasingly evident.
Jiāng Shí proposed deposing the emperor
and installing Prince Bǎo Xuán of Jiāngxià.
Liú Xuān had once served as the administrative officer for Bǎo Xuán in Yǐngzhōu,
and his handling of affairs was excessively harsh.
Someone presented a horse,
and Bǎo Xuán wished to see it.
Xuān said:
“What use is there in looking at a horse!”
When someone requested boiled pork,
and the attendants consulted Xuān,
he said:
“We already boiled a goose this morning;
there’s no need for this again.”
Bǎo Xuán angrily said:
“My uncle truly lacks the affection of Wèiyáng.”
The preface to the poem “Wèiyáng” says: The mother of Duke Kāng of Qín
was a daughter of Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
Duke Wén encountered the disaster caused by Lí Jī,
and before he could return,
his Qin-born mother passed away.
Duke Mù welcomed Duke Wén.
Duke Kāng, then the crown prince,
escorted Duke Wén to the north bank of the Wèi River.
Grieving that he could no longer see his mother,
he said, “When I see my maternal uncle,
it is as if my mother were still alive.”
Liú Xuān
was the younger brother of Emperor Míng’s Empress Liú,
so Bǎo Xuán addressed him as “uncle.”
Now, according to the minor preface of the poem regarding the Wèiyáng incident,
it was the nephew who showed affection toward his uncle.
Later generations generally refer to an uncle who fails to show affection toward his nephew as lacking “Wèiyáng affection,”
which is mistaken.
“Huì” (恚)
is pronounced “yú bì fān.”
He disagreed with Shí’s proposal
and instead wished to install Prince Bǎo Yín of Jiàn’ān.
Shí secretly consulted Prince Yáo Guāng of Shǐ’ān,
but Yáo Guāng, considering himself the elder,
desired the throne for himself
and hinted at this to sway Shí.
Shí’s younger brother Sì also believed that a young ruler would be difficult to maintain,
so he urged Shí to support Yáo Guāng.
Shí’s mind became hesitant and confused.
He asked Xiāo Tǎnzhī for advice.
Tǎnzhī was then in mourning for his mother,
but had been recalled to serve as General of the Central Army.
“Recalled” means
he was summoned from his mourning hut
to resume his official position.
“Emperor Míng’s accession
was already irregular,
and the realm has never accepted it.
If we do this again,
I fear the four corners will disintegrate.
I dare not speak of the consequences.”
He then returned home to continue his mourning.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī was obsessed with glory and power;
how could he truly complete the mourning period!
It was simply because the matter of deposing and installing an emperor was of great importance
that he did not wish to be involved in its calamities,
using this as a pretext to withdraw and avoid it.
Shí and Sì secretly said to the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, Xiè Tiǎo:
“The Prince of Jiāngxià is young;
if he proves unable to bear the burden,
how could we depose and install again!
The Prince of Shǐ’ān is older;
his succession would not contradict public expectations.
We do not seek wealth and honor through this,
but only wish to secure the state.”
“Zhèng” (政) here is the same as “zhèng” (正).
They wished to draw him into their faction,
but Tiǎo did not respond.
Shortly after,
Yáo Guāng appointed Tiǎo to concurrently oversee the affairs of the Commandant of the Guards.
Tiǎo became fearful.
For a Vice Director to concurrently hold a ministerial post
was in itself nothing to fear;
what he feared was
that he was being used by Yáo Guāng
and would thus suffer calamity.
Xīng Shèng did not dare to act.
Tiǎo also advised Liú Xuān, saying:
“If the Prince of Shǐ’ān ascends the throne,
then Liú Fán and Liú Yàn will occupy your current positions as ministers,
and they will only regard you as a fickle man.”
Yàn was
Yáo Guāng’s City Defense Army Advisor.
Xuān feigned shock
and rushed to inform Yáo Guāng and Shí.
Yáo Guāng wanted to send Tiǎo out to serve as Administrator of Dōngyáng Commandery,
but Tiǎo had often looked down upon Shí.
Xiè Tiǎo, due to his family background, looked down upon Jiāng Shí.
Yáo Guāng then had Tiǎo arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review.
Together with Xiào Sì, Shí, Xuān, and others, he jointly submitted a memorial stating:
“Tiǎo stirred up trouble inside and outside the court,
recklessly disparaged the imperial carriage,
secretly discussed palace prohibitions,
slandered close and worthy relatives,
and lightly criticized court ministers.”
Tiǎo then died in prison.
Xuān believed that if Yáo Guāng were installed,
he would lose the status of being the emperor’s maternal uncle,
so he refused to agree with Shí’s proposal.
Therefore, Shí hesitated and could not decide for a long time.
Yáo Guāng was greatly angered
and sent his attendant Huáng Tánqìng to assassinate Xuān at Qīngxī Bridge.
Tánqìng saw that Xuān had many guards,
and dared not act.
Xuān became aware of it
and thus exposed Shí’s plot.
The emperor ordered Shí and his brothers arrested.
At that time, Sì was on duty in the inner palace.
Suspecting something amiss,
he sent a messenger to report to Shí, saying:
“Liú Xuān seems to have treacherous intentions.
What plan should we make now?”
Shí said:
“We should simply remain calm to stabilize the situation.”
Soon an edict arrived summoning Shí for an audience.
He was detained in the Central Secretariat.
Earlier,
Yuán Wénkuàng was due to be enfeoffed for his merit in beheading Wáng Jìngzé.
(The beheading of Jìngzé
is recorded in the first scroll of Emperor Míng’s Yǒngtài era.)
At that time, Cuī Gōngzǔ, for having stabbed Jìngzé,
contested the merit with Wénkuàng.
Shí insisted on not granting it,
and this was likely the reason.
“Qǔ” (取) here
means to kill him.
“Can he still seize my enfeoffment or not!”
Both he and his younger brother Sì were executed.
When Liú Xuān heard of Shí’s death,
he awoke from sleep in great shock,
leaped out of his room,
and asked his attendants:
“Have the arresting officers arrived yet?”
After a long while,
his mind settled,
and he returned to sit down.
Greatly sorrowful, he said:
“It’s not that I miss Jiāng [Shí],
but I grieve for myself!”
Xuān knew that disaster would soon befall him.
From then on, the emperor had nothing to fear or restrain him,
and he became even more unrestrained.
Day and night, he and his close attendants in the rear hall would shout loudly
and play at horse games.
He often went to bed at the fifth watch
and rose only in the late afternoon.
When officials came for scheduled or monthly morning audiences,
“shuò” (朔)
refers to the first day of each month.
Besides the morning audience on the first day,
there were also other scheduled audience days within the month,
hence called “jié” (節).
Sometimes they were dismissed as darkness fell.
If they came to court in the late afternoon,
the emperor would again not appear,
so they were dismissed as darkness approached.
Matters might be left unreported for tens of days,
or the emperor’s whereabouts might be unknown.
Eunuchs would wrap fish and meat to take home,
using documents from the Five Departments.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
there had been six Ministries of State.
South of the Yangtze, there were the Ministries of Personnel, Rituals, Military, Civil Affairs, and Finance—five Ministers,
each heading a department,
called the Five Departments of the Secretariat.
“Àn” (案) here
refers to official documents;
they were kept as records and evidence.
The Secretariat used yellow paper,
hence called “yellow documents.”
“Zhì” (致) means
extreme;
“shì” (適) means suitable for pleasure.
“Jiāng Shí always forbade me from riding horses;
if that fellow were still alive,
how could I have gotten to do this!”
He then asked:
“Which of Shí’s relatives remain?”
The reply was:
“Jiāng Xiáng is now in Yě.”
The emperor had executed Shí and his brothers,
but Xiáng alone was spared death and exiled to Dōngyě.
The emperor then ordered Xiáng to commit suicide.
Prince Shǐ'ān Wáng Xiāo Yáoguāng had long harbored rebellious ambitions.
He secretly plotted with his younger brother, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Yáoxīn, to raise troops and seize control of the Eastern Administrative Headquarters.
He sent Yáoxīn to lead troops swiftly down from Jiānglíng.
The appointed date for the action was approaching,
but then Yáoxīn fell ill and died.
After Jiāng Shí was executed,
the Emperor summoned Yáoguāng into the palace hall,
informing him of Shí's crimes.
Yáoguāng became fearful,
afraid that disaster would reach him.
(The term "Shěng" here refers to the Zhōngshū Shěng.)
Yáoguāng was then serving as Zhōngshū Lìng.
He then claimed illness and no longer entered the Táichéng.
He returned to the Eastern Administrative Headquarters.
He then claimed illness and no longer entered the Táichéng.
(The pronunciation of "hào" is...)
...hù gāo fān.
Yáoguāng's younger brother, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Yáochāng, died,
and all his troops returned to Yáoguāng.
When Yáoxīn's funeral procession returned,
it halted at the front islet of the Eastern Administrative Headquarters.
The forces from Jīngzhōu escorting it were very numerous.
(The "front islet" is...)
...an islet in the Qínhuái River.
The Eastern Administrative Headquarters faced the Qínhuái River.
Fearing that Yáoguāng felt insecure,
(the court) intended to transfer him to be Sītú,
and have him return to his residence.
Transferring him to Sītú was to elevate his position and prestige,
while having him return to his residence was to recuperate from illness.
Yáoguāng feared being killed.
On the day Yǐmǎo, in the late afternoon,
he gathered the troops from the two provinces at the east gate of the Eastern Administrative Headquarters.
(The "troops from the two provinces" refers to...)
...those who came from Jīngzhōu and Yùzhōu.
Using the pretext of attacking Liú Xuān.
At night,
he sent several hundred men to break into the Eastern Ironworks,
releasing the prisoners,
and seizing weapons from the Imperial Workshops.
("Zhàng" refers to...)
...weapons.
Yuán Lìshēng followed the summons and arrived.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī's residence was east of the Eastern Administrative Headquarters city.
Yáoguāng sent men to seize him by surprise.
Tǎnzhī, with his hair loose and upper body bare, climbed over the wall and fled.
("Lù" means...)
...hair worn loose/unbound.
("Tǎn" means...)
...baring the upper body.
He ran towards the Táichéng,
wanting to enter and report the matter.
(The "Patrol Captain" was...)
...an officer leading troops patrolling outside the Táichéng walls.
(The pronunciation of "luó" is...)
...láng zuǒ fān.
Seeing Tǎnzhī bare-chested and fleeing with his body exposed,
(the captain) suspected he was a criminal escaping,
so he arrested him.
(Tǎnzhī) told him about Yáoguāng's rebellion,
(but the captain) did not believe him.
He went himself to investigate and inquire,
learned the truth,
then gave Tǎnzhī a horse,
and followed him into the Táichéng.
Yáoguāng also sent men to seize Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Shěn Wénjì from his residence,

but it happened that Wénjì had already entered the Táichéng.
Yuán Lìshēng advised Yáoguāng to lead the troops inside the city to attack the Táichéng at night,
using carts of reeds to burn the city gates,
saying:
"My lord, you just ride in the carriage and follow behind.
("Yù" is the same as "yú".)
Yáoguāng hesitated and did not dare to go out.
As dawn gradually broke,
Yáoguāng, in military attire, came out to the audience hall,
ordered weapons distributed, mounted the city walls, and distributed rewards.
Lìshēng again urged sending out the army,
but Yáoguāng refused,
hoping for a spontaneous change within the Táichéng.
When the sun rose,
the Táichéng army gradually arrived.
Within the Táichéng, they first heard of the disorder,
and the mood of the crowd was anxious and confused.
As dawn approached,
an edict was issued summoning Xú Xiàosì.
Xiàosì entered,
and only then did people's hearts settle.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Shěn Yuē heard of the disturbance.
According to the Liáng Shū biography of Shěn Yuē,
Yuē was then Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Here the character
"wèi"
is missing.
Some advised him to wear military attire.
Yuē said:
"The Táichéng is currently in turmoil.
If they see me in military attire,
some might think I am siding with Yáoguāng."
So he entered wearing red robes.
On the day Bǐngchén,
an edict was issued granting a special amnesty to Jiànkāng,
and a state of alert was declared inside and outside.
Xú Xiàosì and those below him garrisoned and guarded the palace city.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī led the Táichéng army to attack Yáoguāng.
Xiàosì inwardly harbored doubts and fears.
He and Shěn Wénjì, both in military attire, sat together atop the Nányē Gate,
wanting to discuss current affairs with him.
But Wénjì repeatedly diverted the conversation to other topics,
so (Xiàosì) never managed to broach the subject.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī was stationed at Xiānggōng Temple.
(Xiānggōng Temple was...)
...built by Emperor Míng of the Sòng dynasty.
The six outer gates of the Táichéng's outer wall only had wicker gates,
lacking an outer wall.
The Eastern Administrative Headquarters was east of the Táichéng,
so (the court) ordered (Zhāng) Xīngshèng to garrison the Eastern Wicker Gate to attack Yáoguāng.
According to Cáo Hǔ's biography: The Great Bridge
is the Middle Bridge over the Qīngxī Stream.
(The Táichéng army) set fire to the three sides of the Sītú's office complex.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
Prince Péngchéng Liú Yìkāng served as Sītú,
moved to reside at the Eastern Administrative Headquarters,
and built the Sītú's office complex beside the Eastern Administrative Headquarters.
The Táichéng army suffered repeated defeats,
and its commander Sāng Tiān'ài was killed.
When Yáoguāng started his uprising,
he consulted his advisor Cānyījūn Xiāo Chàng.
Chàng sternly refused to comply.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Chàng and Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ Shěn Zhāolüè secretly slipped out from the south gate,
went to the Táichéng and surrendered themselves,
greatly demoralizing the troops' morale.
(This refers to the morale within the Eastern Administrative Headquarters.)
(The pronunciation of "jǔ" is...)
...zài lǚ fān.
(Xiāo Chàng was) Xiāo Yǎn's younger brother;
(Shěn) Zhāolüè was
...the son of Wénjì's elder brother.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Yuán Lìshēng went out from the south gate to fight,
then abandoned his lance and surrendered to Cáo Hǔ,
who ordered him executed.
Yáoguāng was furious.
He leaped up and down on his bed,
and had Lìshēng's son killed.
That evening,
the Táichéng army used fire arrows to burn the northeastern corner tower.
By night,
the city walls collapsed.
Yáoguāng returned to the small study within his tent,
put on his robe and cap and sat down,
held a candle to illuminate himself,
and ordered people to bar the door from the inside.
The study's doors and gates were all heavily barred.
His attendants all climbed over the roof and scattered away.
The Táichéng army commander Liú Guóbǎo and others entered first.
Yáoguāng heard outside soldiers arriving,
extinguished the candle and crawled under the bed.
Soldiers pushed open the door and entered,
dragged him out from the darkness,
and beheaded him.
The Táichéng army entered the city,
and burned the buildings almost completely.
Liú Fàn fled back home,
but was killed by someone.
The Jīngzhōu general Pān Shào heard that Yáoguāng had started a rebellion,
and plotted to respond to him.
(He intended to have Jiānglíng respond.)
(The pronunciation of "jiàng" is...)
...jí liàng fān.
At that time, Prince Nánkāng Xiāo Bǎoróng, as West Central General, was garrisoning Jiānglíng,
with Xiàhóu Xiáng as his Military Advisor.
(The pronunciation of "Xià" is...)
...hù yǎ fān.
(Xiáng) then had (Pān Shào) executed,
and the province and commandery administration was pacified.
("Zhōu" refers to...)
...Jīngzhōu;
"Fǔ" refers to
...the West Central General's headquarters.
On the day Jǐsì,
(the court) appointed Xú Xiàosì as Sīkōng;
added to Shěn Wénjì the title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,

(Shěn Wénjì was given the additional title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,

(Xiāo Tǎnzhī's position of) Yòu Jiāngjūn remained as before;

After Yáoguāng was pacified,

Cáo Hǔ was made Sànqí Chángshì and Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn;

18. Shěn Líng, the Southern Xúzhōu Regional Inspector of Wèi, came to surrender.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Wèi established Southern Xúzhōu at Sùyù.
Surrender,
pronounced as *hù jiāng fān*.
He was a clansman of Shěn Wénjì.
Shěn Wénxiù defended Dōngyáng for Sòng,

Wénxiù
was a cousin of Wénjì;
Líng's entry into Wèi
likely occurred around that time.
All administrative matters were decided by Chief Clerk Lú Yuān.
Yuān knew Líng was about to rebel,

means to warn.
The Wèi court did not heed him.
Líng then killed his officers,
and led the troops of Sùyù to come and submit,

Líng had been on the border for years,
secretly allying with local magnates in the border prefectures.
After Líng rebelled,
many commanderies and counties arrested and sent in Líng's partisans,

placing the blame solely on Líng,
thus calming the public mind.
If roots were connected and branches implicated,
then the magnates along the border, fearing punishment,

19. In the intercalary month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Jiānglíng Duke Bǎo Lǎn was established as Prince of Shǐ'ān,

Since Yáoguāng had been executed,

The eldest son of Dào Shēng, Prince Zhēn of Shǐ'ān, Fèng, died during the Sòng era.

Yáoguāng
was the son of the Reverent Prince.
20. Shěn Líng was appointed as Northern Xúzhōu Regional Inspector.
Qí's Southern Xúzhōu was administered from Jīngkǒu,

the Emperor's attendants, the "sword-bearers" and "edict-responders," all acted arbitrarily and wielded power,
and people of the time called them

"Commander of Yánmíng"

Ruthless,
pronounced *hù kěn fān*.
Favored,

Cousin,

"Emperor Míng was Emperor Wǔ's cousin,
Emperor Míng,

Tǎnzhī,
Hǔ newly appointed officials,

Yángpíng King Xīnchéng,
