Lǐ Yánshòu said: Wáng Yù was originally a Qiāng from the Lǐ Rùn Garrison in Féngyì.
His ancestors were a powerful clan among the Qiāng,
and they claimed the surname Wáng.
Later, they changed it to the Qián'ěr clan,
and by the time of Wèi Xuānwǔ,
they reverted to Wáng.
He was punished with castration for an offense,
and gradually rose to become Minister of Personnel,
with the title of Duke of Dàngchāng.
"Your Highness,
the Duke of Zhōu of the state,
supports and balances the royal house.
Āhéng,
refers to someone like Yī Yǐn.
Zhèng Xuán said: Ā,
means to rely on;
héng,
means to balance.
Yī Yǐn was relied upon by Tāng to achieve balance,
hence it was used as an official title.
You should naturally comply with the imperial will;
guān zhǐ,
means to report to and follow the imperial will.
You are harming the public to benefit the private!"
Yù was both uneasy,
and Xiáng also felt ashamed and apologized.
Zhōng often incurred Xiáng's anger due to his forthrightness and integrity.
Xiáng once scolded Zhōng, saying:
"I worry that I will see you die first,
and not worry that you will see the time of my death!"
Zhōng said:
"In this life,
everyone has a predetermined fate.
If I am destined to die by Your Highness's hand,
avoiding it would be futile;
if not,
Your Highness cannot kill me!"
Zhōng, for his merits in suppressing Prince of Xiányáng Xǐ,
was enfeoffed as Duke of Wèijùn,
promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and concurrently served as General of the Martial Guards.
Xiáng took advantage of Zhōng's petition to decline the enfeoffment,
and secretly advised the Wèi emperor to appoint Zhōng as one of the Nine Ministers,
to remove him from the emperor's side,
and relieve him of his positions as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of the Martial Guards,
roles that kept him constantly by the emperor's side.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to halt his enfeoffment,
and he was honorably promoted to Minister of the Imperial Treasury.
Xiáng was able to use strategy to distance Yú Zhōng,
but did not realize that Gāo Zhǎo had already planned his downfall.
32 Duke Xiāo Yǐngzhòu of Bādōng, due to the stalemate between Xiāo Guī and Cài Dàogōng,
became worried and indignant, falling ill:
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu saw that Xiāo Yǎn's eastern campaign
was victorious wherever it went,
while he himself, assisting Prince Nánkāng in Jiānglíng,
could not control Xiāo Guī nearby;
externally, he had no way to subdue the hearts of treacherous and ambitious men, and internally, he faced enemies close at hand.
This was why worry and indignation led to illness.
Guī,
pronunciation gǔ huí fān.
On Rénwǔ,
he died.
Xiàhóu Xiáng kept it secret,
having someone with similar handwriting forge orders in his name,
and secretly reported it to Xiāo Yǎn,
who also kept it secret.
Xiáng conscripted troops from Yōngzhōu,
and Xiāo Wěi sent Xiāo Dàn to lead troops to assist.
When Guī and others heard that Jiànkāng was already in danger,
their troops became fearful and dispersed,
and both Guī and Lǔ Xiūliè surrendered.
Only then was Yǐngzhòu's death announced,
and he was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Chancellor.
Thereupon, all hopes turned to Yǎn.
Xiàhóu Xiáng requested to jointly participate in military and state affairs with Xiāo Dàn.
An edict appointed Xiáng as Palace Attendant and Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Soon after, he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General Who Pacifies the Army, and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Xiáng firmly yielded the position to Dàn.
Thus, Dàn was appointed to administer the military affairs of the Jīngzhōu government.
33 Wèi rebuilt the circular mound altar on the north bank of the Yī River;
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Qímíngdì,
Wèi Xiàowén had established the circular mound altar at Wěisù Mountain.
Now it was changed.
The Classic of Waterways states: The Yī River originates from Xúnqú Mountain west of Nányáng County,
flows northeast past Lùhún Xīnchéng County,
then northeast through the Yīquè Pass,
and further northeast to the south of Luòyáng County, where it turns north and flows into the Luò River.
Wèi likely established the circular mound altar south of Luòyáng,
on the north bank of the Yī River.
On Yǐmǎo,
sacrifices were first offered there.
34 Wèi General Who Guards the South Yuán Yīng submitted a memorial stating:
"Xiāo Bǎojuǎn grows increasingly reckless and indulgent by the day,
cruelly harming the innocent.
His Governor of Yōngzhōu, Xiāo Yǎn, is marching east to attack Mòlíng,
mobilizing all his forces,
and advancing downstream;
leaving only an isolated city,
with no additional defenses.
This means Xiāngyáng is empty.
It is a rare opportunity that comes once in an age;
if we do not seize this chance,
what are we waiting for!
I beg to personally lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
heading directly to Miǎnyīn.
Xiāngyáng is south of the Miǎn River;
the south bank of a river is yīn.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
We will cut off the route at Hēishuǐ.

with us positioned upstream,

Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said: There are three Chǔ: the customs from Huái, Pèi, Chén, Rǔnán, and Nánjùn
constitute Western Chǔ;
east of Péngchéng,

They would be like fish swimming in a cauldron,

if this opportunity is missed,
shuǎng,
means to err.
The matter was shelved and no reply was given.
The General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yuán Huái, submitted a memorial stating:
“Xiāo Yǎn is committing internal aggression,
while Bǎo Juǎn is isolated and in peril.
The garrisons at Guǎnglíng, Huáiyīn, and other places are all watching to see who gains or loses.
This is truly a Heaven-sent opportunity,
a moment for annexation.

If Xiāo Yǎn succeeds,

Why is that?
Shòuchūn is only seven hundred lǐ from Jiànkāng.
Wèi established Yángzhōu at Shòuchūn,
as seen in the previous scroll, last year.
This is all familiar to them.
If they are secure internally and externally,

Now, Bǎo Juǎn’s capital faces the danger of collapse,

To clear the region south of the Yangtze,
the time is precisely today.”

The Wèi sovereign then appointed Rénchéng Wáng Chéng as Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Huáinán, General-in-Chief Who Guards the South, Holder of the Third Rank with Equal Status to the Three Excellencies, and Governor of Yángzhōu,
entrusting him with the strategy.
However, this was ultimately not carried out.
Had Wèi followed the plans of these two ministers,
drawing the Yangtze as the border,
it would not have had to wait for the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng.
Rén,
pronounced as rén.
He was the son of Hè.
Yuán Hè,
the son of Tūfǎ Rùtán,
entered Wèi service,
and was granted the surname Yuán.
The Governor of Dōngyùzhōu, Tián Yìzōng, submitted a memorial stating:
“The Xiāo clan has thrown norms into chaos,
with ruler and ministers contending against each other.
The provinces and garrisons south of the Yangtze
are split into two halves,

The common people are exhausted by transport duties,

passes northeast through Tóngbǎi Mountain,
then flows east past Yìyáng County,
hence it is said Yìyáng is relatively close to the source of the Huái.
The source of the Huái is shallow and narrow,
making this area an advantageous crossing point and strategic passage for Wèi troops on campaign.
If military action occurs beyond the Huái,

he will inevitably use troops beyond the Huái.
Deploying boats along the long Huái;
this refers to the typical military posture of Jiāngnán.
Fàn cháng,
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
They must come from north of Yìyáng,
this refers to the route for Wèi troops heading to Shòuchūn.
Wèi,
refers to Yìyáng.
The subjugation of Yìyáng,
the time is truly now.
I estimate they require no more than twelve thousand elite troops;
however, the method of conducting campaigns
values displaying formidable posture.
I request that the forces of the two Jīng provinces make a westward feint towards Suí and Yōng,
the two Jīng,
refers to Wèi establishing Jīngzhōu at Rǎngchéng and Dōngjīngzhōu at Bǐyáng.
Suí and Yōng,
refer to Suí Commandery and Xiāngyáng.
Yōng,
pronounced yú yòng fān.
To block reinforcements from the Three Passes;
then the armies of the two Yù provinces can directly occupy Nánguān,
confronting Yántóu,
the two Yù,
refers to Wèi establishing Yùzhōu at Rǔnán and Dōngyùzhōu at Xīnxī.
Nánguān,

Yántóu,

If we advance the army in late winter,

it will take no more than one hundred days,

Textual Analysis Notes: The biography of Yìzōng states:
“Emperor Shìzōng accepted this,
and dispatched Yuán Yīng to attack Yìyáng.”
According to records, Yīng attacked Yìyáng in the eighth month of the fourth year of the Jǐngmíng era.
This memorial speaks of the Xiāo clan’s ruler and ministers contending,
which was during Liáng Wǔ’s attack on Dōnghūn.
It seems Yìzōng proposed this strategy at this time,
but it was implemented two years later.
“Now Bǎo Juǎn’s own flesh and blood are harming each other,
and the frontier garrisons stand in a tripartite division.
Yìyáng is isolated and cut off,
close to Your Majesty’s territory.
Internally, it lacks secure military stores,
externally, it has no scheduled grain reinforcements.
This is like a bird about to be burned,
we cannot remove the firewood;
it is an enemy offering its head,
how can we delay the axe!
If we miss this chance and do not take it,
not only will future campaigns be difficult to plan,
I also fear it may become a deeper trouble.
Now, the Governor of Yùzhōu, Sīmǎ Yuè, has already made preparations and is about to set out.
The Governor of Dōngyùzhōu, Tián Yìzōng, has troops guarding the Three Passes.

The Wèi sovereign then sent the Attendant of the Imperial Bedchamber, Yáng Língyǐn, to serve as Military Controller.
Attendant of the Imperial Bedchamber,
a title derived from serving in the imperial bedchamber.

Sòng had a Jiànníng Left Commandery.
In the eighth year of the Xiàowǔ Emperor’s Dàmíng era,
Jiànníng Left Commandery was abolished and made Jiànníng County,
belonging to Xīyáng Commandery,
later restored as a commandery.
The Suī History records: Máchéng County of Huángzhōu,
formerly had Jiànníng Commandery established.
Also,
in the twenty-fifth year of Sòng Wéndì’s Yuánjiā era,
twenty-eight counties were established with the barbarian people of the Yù region,
Chìtíng being one of them.
Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jǔ River flows south from the city of Húbēi,
passes by Chìtíng below,
called the Chìtíng River.
Among the Five Rivers barbarians of Xīyáng,
Chìtíng is one of them.
Textual Analysis Notes: The Wèi Imperial Annals state:
“On the yǐwèi day of the seventh month,
Tián Yìzōng defeated Xiāo Bǎo Juǎn’s general Huáng Tiāncì at Chìtíng.”
The biography of Tián Yìguāng states:
“In the early years of the Jǐngmíng era,
Xiāo Yǎn dispatched the Army Commander Wú Zǐyáng to lead troops to raid the Three Passes.
Yìzōng sent the Grand Administrator of Guāngchéng, Méi Yǔzhī, to occupy Chángfēng City and engage Zǐyáng,
defeating him soundly,
beheading and capturing over a thousand.”
According to records, Wú Zǐyáng was a general of Dōnghūn,
not a general of Yǎn.
Moreover, Yǎn was at that time confronting Dōnghūn,
how would he have spare time to raid Wèi’s Three Passes!
This must be an error in Yìzōng’s biography.
“Yìguāng’s biography”
should be
“Yìzōng’s biography”.
35 When Cuī Huìjǐng pressed upon Jiànkāng,

Dōnghūn Hóu appointed Jiǎng Zǐwén as Acting Yellow Axe, Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Prime Minister, Grand Tutor, General-in-Chief, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Governor of Yángzhōu, and Prince of Zhōngshān.
When Yǎn arrived,
he further honored Zǐwén as Divine Emperor,
moved the deity’s image into the rear hall,
and had shamans pray and offer sacrifices to seek blessings.
When the city gates were closed,
all military affairs within the city were entrusted to Wáng Zhēnguó.
The Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Zhāng Jì, entered to guard the capital,
with Jì appointed as Zhēnguó’s deputy.
Jì
was the younger brother of Zhāng Huái.
Zhāng Huái was at that time Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments.
At that time, the city still had seventy thousand armored soldiers.
Dōng Hūn had always been fond of military formations.
Together with eunuchs, knife attendants, and palace women, he practiced combat in front of the Huáguāng Hall.
He pretended to be wounded,
and had people carry him away on a plank,
using this as a ritual to ward off evil.
He often wore military attire in the hall and rode horses in and out,
with armor and helmets made of gold and silver,
adorned with kǒngcuì.
Kǒng and cuì
refer to peacocks and kingfishers.
Armor
is pronounced kǎi.
Everything was as usual.
Hearing the sound of drums and shouts from outside,
he put on a large red robe,
climbed onto the roof of the Jǐngyáng Tower to look out.
The present-day Fǎbǎo Temple in Jiànkāng
is the former site of the Jǐngyáng Tower.
The character 被
is pronounced pī.
Initially,
Dōng Hūn and his attendants plotted,
believing that Chén Xiǎndá was defeated in a single battle,
and Cuī Huìjǐng, who besieged the city, soon fled.
They thought Dǎng Yǎn’s troops would be the same,
so they ordered the imperial kitchen to prepare firewood and rice for only a hundred days.
After the defeat at Dàhéng,
the people were terrified.
Rú Fǎzhēn and others, fearing that soldiers and civilians would flee and scatter,
closed the city gates and no longer sent troops out.
Soon, a long siege was established,
with trenches and barricades tightly fortified.
Only then did they venture out to fight,
but they were repeatedly defeated in battle.
Dōng Hūn was especially stingy with money,
unwilling to give rewards.
Fǎzhēn kowtowed and pleaded with him,
but Dōng Hūn said:
"If the rebels come, will they only take me?
Why come to me asking for things!"
There were hundreds of wooden planks stored in the rear hall,
which were requested for city defense.
Dōng Hūn wanted to keep them for palace construction,
and ultimately did not give them.
He also ordered the imperial workshop to make three hundred sets of fine weapons,
to be used for clearing the palace after the siege was lifted.
Gold and silver carvings and miscellaneous items
were demanded even more urgently than usual.
Everyone was resentful and懈怠,
and did not put in their best effort.
As the siege dragged on,
everyone in the city longed for an early end,
but no one dared to take the initiative.
Rú Fǎzhēn and Méi Chóng’ér advised Dōng Hūn:
"The ministers are not paying attention,
allowing the siege to continue.
They should all be executed."
Wáng Zhēnguó and Zhāng Jì, fearing disaster,
secretly sent a trusted person to offer a bright mirror to Xiāo Yǎn.
Yǎn broke a piece of gold in response.
A mirror is used to reflect things;
offering a mirror
meant they wanted Yǎn to see their hearts.
The Great Commentary of the Yìjīng says: When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal.
Thus, Yǎn used this as his response.
The character 断
is pronounced duàn,
and Wáng Sù pronounced it as dīng guǎn.
Zhāng Qí,
who was Jì’s trusted confidant,
was approached by Zhēnguó through Qí to secretly plot with Jì
to assassinate Dōng Hūn together.
Qí led Zhēnguó to Jì at night,
and they knelt together to finalize the plan.
Qí himself held the candle;
he also informed the rear chamber attendant Qián Qiáng of the plan.
The rear chamber attendant
was likely established during the Jiāngzuǒ period,
to oversee the rear chambers of the palace.
According to records, the rear chamber attendant
often stayed within the palace,
as seen in the case of Xú Lóngjū.
On the night of Bǐngyín,
Qiáng secretly ordered someone to open the Yúnlóng Gate.
Zhēnguó and Jì led troops into the hall,
with the imperial guard Fēng Yǒngzhī acting as an insider.
Fēng Yǒngzhī
was a soldier of the Right Guard,
trusted by Dōng Hūn.
According to the genealogy of surnames, the surname Fēng
originated from the descendants of Zǐ Fēng of the Zhèng Qī Mù.
Dōng Hūn was not yet fully asleep
when he heard soldiers entering.
He rushed out through the north door,
intending to return to the rear palace,
but the door was already closed.
The eunuch Huáng Tàipíng wounded his knee with a knife,
causing him to fall to the ground.
Zhāng Qí then beheaded him.
Dōng Hūn was nineteen years old at the time.
Officials were ordered to sign a petition,
and Dōng Hūn’s head was wrapped in yellow oil.
Yellow silk coated with oil could repel rain,
and was called yellow oil.
Wrapping something in yellow oil
allowed the inside to be visible from the outside,
likely to make it easier for Xiāo Yǎn to inspect.
A note on discrepancies: The Nánshǐ Wáng Liàng biography states:
"Zhāng Jì and others discussed establishing Xiāngdōng’s heir, Bǎo Zhì.

This account follows the Qí Jì.
"Even if a crown is worn out,
how can it be placed on one’s feet!"
He took leaves from the courtyard tree, rubbed them, and swallowed them,
pretending to be unconscious,
and did not sign his name.
When Yǎn read the petition and saw no name from Zhì,
he inwardly praised him.
Liàng
was Yíng’s younger cousin;
Zhì
was the son of Sēngqián.
Wáng Yíng
was appointed by Xiāo Yǎn as Left Chief Clerk of the Chancellor’s Office.

held a high position in the early Qí dynasty.
Yǎn and Yún once traveled together to the Western Lodge of Jìnglíng,
as recorded in the second year of Yǒngmíng of Emperor Wǔ’s reign, scroll 136.
Wáng Liàng, during Dōng Hūn’s reign,
accommodated others to secure his position.
When Xiāo Yǎn reached Xīnlín,
all officials secretly sent messages pledging allegiance,

After Dōng Hūn’s defeat,
Liàng went out to meet Yǎn.
Yǎn said:
"If one does not support someone who has fallen,

Liàng replied:
"If he could have been supported,
would you, Lord, have taken action today?"
The Analects record
Confucius saying:
"If one does not support someone in danger,
or help someone who has fallen,
then what use is such a minister?"
Yǎn used this to question Wáng Liàng.
Some were robbed or stripped of their belongings.
Yáng Gōngzé personally led his troops to form ranks at the Eastern Side Gate,
escorting officials, scholars, and commoners.
Thus, many who left passed through Gōngzé’s camp.
Yǎn sent Zhāng Hóngcè to first enter and clear the palace,
sealing the treasury and archives.
At that time, treasures were piled up in the city.
Hóngcè strictly forbade his troops
from taking even the slightest thing.
He arrested Pān and the favored ministers Rú Fǎzhēn, Méi Chóng’ér, Wáng Xuǎnzhī, and forty-one others, handing them over to the authorities.
36 Initially,
when Hǎilíng King was deposed,
as recorded in the first year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Míng’s reign, scroll 139,
it was named Xuāndé Palace.
On Yǐsì,
Xiāo Yǎn, under the order of Empress Dowager Xuāndé, posthumously deposed Fúlíng King as Marquis Dōng Hūn,

Yǎn was appointed as Central Inspector, Grand Marshal, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Yángzhōu,

all officials paid their respects.

Xiāo Yǎn’s intentions
were known to all,
so why wait for Fàn Yún and Shěn Yuē to initiate it?
The matter of Wǔlíng King Zūn
is recorded in the third year of Yuánxīng of Jìn Emperor Ān’s reign, scroll 113.
On Rénshēn,
Bǎo Yín, Prince of Jiàn’ān, was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Póyáng.
On Guǐyǒu,
Bǎo Yì, Prince of Jìn’ān, who served as Minister Over the Masses and Governor of Yángzhōu, was appointed as Grand Commandant,
concurrently serving as Minister Over the Masses.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
Xiāo Yǎn entered and stationed himself at the Yuèwǔ Hall,
issuing an order for a general amnesty.
He also issued an order:
"All oppressive regulations, unjust taxes, cruel punishments, and excessive corvée labor, aside from these,
should be thoroughly examined as to their original causes,
and completely abolished;
'Yuán' (原),
in the Nánshǐ, is written as
'Yuán' (源).
'Qián yuán' (前源)
refers to the origins of previously initiated affairs.
'Dàng' (盪)
is written as
'Dàng' (蕩),
pronounced with the sound 'tǔ lǎng fān'.
Carefully establish regulations and articles,
all following the principle of leniency."
Yuán (原)
means to pardon.
Shǒu (守),
is also pronounced 'shì yòu fān'.
"Thoroughly examine all bureaus of the Shàngshū Department;
for all unjust lawsuits and disputes during the time of the Dōng Hūn Emperor,

conduct careful interrogations and distinctions,

Xùn (讯)
means to question.

Biàn (辩)
means to distinguish clearly.

Biàn (辩),
is pronounced 'bīng miǎn fān'.
"Bury the righteous troops,
and inter the dead among the rebellious followers."
Pān (潘) possessed beauty surpassing the state,
Xiāo Yǎn wanted to keep her,
and asked Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Mào about it,
Wáng Mào said:
"This thing caused the downfall of Qí,

So she was strangled to death in prison,
and along with her, the favored minister Rú Fǎzhēn and others were executed.
Two thousand palace women were distributed as rewards to the officers and soldiers.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Xiāo Hóng was appointed as Zhōnghùjūn.
When Xiāo Yǎn advanced eastward,
the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Xiānpín held troops and did not submit to Xiāo Yǎn,
Xiāo Yǎn sent his old acquaintance Yáo Zhòngbīn to persuade him,
Mǎ Xiānpín first set up wine for him,
then beheaded him at the army gate as a warning.
Xiāo Yǎn also sent his clansman uncle Huáiyuǎn to persuade him,
Mǎ Xiānpín said:
"For great righteousness, one should disregard family ties,"
and wanted to behead him as well;
the army pleaded for him,
and he was spared.
When Xiāo Yǎn reached Xīnlín,
Mǎ Xiānpín was still on the west bank of the river, daily plundering transport ships.
The seat of Yùzhōu was at Lìyáng,
located west of the great river.
Chāo (抄),
is pronounced 'chǔ jiāo fān'.
The various provinces and commanderies all sent envoys requesting to surrender,
but the Wúxīng Tàishǒu Yuán Áng alone defended his borders and did not accept the order.
Yuán Áng
was the son of Yuán Yǐ.
Yuán Yǐ died during the Yìjiā calamity.
Cáo Wèi established twenty-three Láng positions,
Jiàbù was one of them.
Dù Yòu said: During Sòng and Qí, Jiàbù was under the Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
"Since the root is already toppled,
how can the branches and leaves remain attached?
Now, exhausting one's strength for a foolish ruler
does not suffice as loyalty;
having one's family slaughtered,
cannot be called filial piety.
Why not instead change course decisively,
and secure much fortune for yourself!"
Yuán Áng replied in a letter:
"The Sānwú region is inland,
not a place for military operations;
moreover, with a single commandery in a remote corner,
what can it accomplish!
Since learning of your banners arriving here,
all have bared their shoulders and approached the army gate on their knees.
'Xī tǎn' (膝袒)
means to bare the shoulder and approach on the knees.
It is precisely because, considering my own mediocrity and simplicity,
lacking both civil and military talents,
even if I wished to offer my heart,
it would not increase the general's courage;
maintaining my foolish silence,
would it hinder the army's prestige?
Fortunately, relying on the general's great magnanimity,
I can proceed with courtesy and composure.
I consider that even for a minor favor like a single meal,
one would still repay with one's life;
how much more so for one who eats another's salary, to suddenly forget it in a single day—
not only would public opinion not permit it,
I also fear you would despise me,
hence my hesitation,
and not yet having the leisure to offer the jade disc."
'Jiàn bì' (荐璧)
means to surrender by holding a jade disc in the mouth.
Jiàn (荐)
means to present.
Wú separated Wúchéng and Yúháng to establish Yǒng'ān County;
in the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn Wǔdì,
it was renamed Wǔkāng,
belonging to Wúxīng Commandery.
"In the past, at the end of the Yuánjiā era,
when there was no opening or path,
the late Tàiwèi gave his life to clarify his integrity.
Yuán Shū was posthumously granted Tàiwèi;
Yuán Shū's death is recorded in scroll 127 of the Sòng Wéndì Yuánjiā thirtieth year.
In principle, there was no thought of preserving oneself,
hence he disregarded danger to follow name and righteousness.
Sītú,
refers to Yuán Áng's father Yuán Yǐ;
Yuán Yǐ's death is recorded in scroll 131 of the Sòng Míngdì Tàishǐ second year.
There has been no repentance or change;
Jīng and Yōng joined forces,
seizing control of the upper reaches,
the intention of Heaven and men is clear.
I hope you, illustrious prefect, will deeply consider this,
and not bring regret upon yourself later."
When Jiànkāng was pacified,
Xiāo Yǎn sent the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Yuánlǚ to pacify and inspect the eastern region,
instructing Lǐ Yuánlǚ:
"Yuán Áng's family is one of pure virtue,
with generations of loyal integrity,
referring to Yuán Shū and Yuán Yǐ.
Do not use military force to oppress or humiliate him."
Lǐ Yuánlǚ arrived at Wúxīng,
and conveyed Xiāo Yǎn's intent;
Yuán Áng still did not request to surrender,
but merely opened the gates and removed the defenses.
Mǎ Xiānpín heard that the imperial city was not held,
wept and said to his officers and soldiers:
"I received a commission from others,
in righteousness I cannot surrender,
you all have parents;
if I am a loyal minister,
and you are filial sons,
would that not be acceptable!"
Then he sent all the troops inside the city out to surrender,
leaving several dozen stalwart men,
to close the gates and hold out alone.
Soon, troops entered,
surrounding them in several tens of layers.
Mǎ Xiānpín ordered his men to all draw their bows fully,
and the soldiers did not dare approach.
At dusk,
Mǎ Xiānpín then threw down his bow and said:
"Gentlemen, just come and take me,
in righteousness I will not surrender."
He was then sent in a cage cart to Shítóu.
Xiāo Yǎn released him,
and had him wait until Yuán Áng arrived to enter together,
saying:
"Let the world see two righteous men."
Xiāo Yǎn said to Mǎ Xiānpín:
"Shooting the hook and cutting the sleeve,
were praised by people of old.
Do not feel remorse for killing the envoy and cutting off supplies."
Mǎ Xiānpín thanked him and said:
"A petty man is like a dog that lost its master,
if a later master feeds it,
then it will serve again."
Xiāo Yǎn laughed,
and treated them both generously.
On the Bǐngxū day,
Xiāo Yǎn entered and took control of the palace halls.
37. After Liú Xīzǔ had captured Ānchéng,
he issued a proclamation to the Xiāng region,
to which Wáng Sēngcàn, the Internal Historian of Shǐxīng, responded.
Sēngcàn declared himself the Governor of Xiāng Province,
and led troops to attack Chángshā.
When they were still over a hundred *li* from the city,
the soldiers from the commanderies and counties of Xiāng Province rose up like a swarm of bees to support Sēngcàn,
with only the four counties of Línxiāng, Xiāngyīn, Liúyáng, and Luó remaining intact.
The two counties of Línxiāng and Luó
had belonged to Chángshā Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.
The state of Wú established Liúyáng County,
which also belonged to Chángshā.
In the second year of the Yuánhuī era of the Sòng Emperor Cāngwú, Xiāngyīn County was established by dividing off parts of Yìyáng, Xiāngxī, and Luó, and incorporating displaced people from Bāxiá,
and it belonged to Xiāngdōng Commandery.
The Suí dynasty changed Línxiāng to Chángshā County,
which became the seat of Tán Prefecture.
The Táng dynasty abolished Luó County, merging it into Xiāngyīn,
which then belonged to Yuè Prefecture.
Liúyáng still belongs to Tán Prefecture today.
The character 瀏
is pronounced *liú*,
and also *liǔ*.
The Administrator Liú Tǎn gathered all their boats and burned them,
and sent the Army Commander Yǐn Fǎlüè to resist Sēngcàn.
After several battles with unfavorable outcomes,
Zhōng Xuánshào, the former Garrison Army Commander of Xiāng Province—
according to the records, there was no such title as Garrison Army Commander among the provincial and prefectural officials at that time,
so this must be an error in the *Liáng Shū*—
set a date to turn the city over in support of Sēngcàn.
Tǎn learned of his plot,
but pretended not to know.
He used the pretext of handling legal cases until late at night,
and left the city gates unclosed to sow doubt.
Before Xuánshào could act,
the next morning,
he went to Tǎn to ask the reason.
Tǎn detained him for a long conversation,
while secretly sending trusted soldiers to search his home.
While Xuánshào was still seated,
the soldiers returned and reported,
having obtained all the documents detailing the plot from beginning to end.
Xuánshào immediately confessed,
and was executed on the spot;
his documents were burned,
and the remaining conspirators were not pursued.
The people felt ashamed and were convinced,
and the province and commanderies were thus pacified.
Fǎlüè and Sēngcàn held each other at bay for several months.
After Jiànkāng city was pacified,
Yáng Gōngzé returned to the province.
Sēngcàn and his followers scattered and fled.
Wáng Dān was killed by the people of the commandery—
Wáng Dān had earlier responded to Liú Xīzǔ with Nánkāng.
Gōngzé was self-restrained, incorruptible, and cautious,
imposing light punishments and low taxes.
Soon after,
the household registrations of Xiāng Province nearly returned to their former numbers.
Punctuated by Niè Chóngqí, proofread by Wáng Chóngwǔ.
